questions.stem: The origin of social and preventive medicine dates back to the:
questions.explanation: The origin of social and preventive medicine dates back to the 18th century. It began even before the germ theory had been proposed.

questions.stem: Which medicine claims to be the world’s first organized body of medical knowledge?
questions.explanation:
Chinese medicine claims to be the world's first organized body of medical knowledge. It dates back to 2700 B.C. They are also considered to be the pioneers of immunization (used variolation against smallpox).
Modern Chinese medicine includes barefoot doctors and acupuncture.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about the ministry of AYUSH except:
options: It was formed in 2014 in India for education and research on AYUSH
It aims to mainstream AYUSH as part of the National Rural Health Mission
It was previously known as department of Indian system of medicine and homeopathy
It regulates the fields of Ayurveda, Yoga, Homeopathy and Siddha only
questions.explanation:
The Ministry of AYUSH was established to regulate the fields of Ayurveda, Yoga, and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy.
It was formed in 2014 in India for the development of education and research in AYUSH. It was previously known as the Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homeopathy (ISM&H). It aims to mainstream AYUSH as part of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM).
The Ayurveda, Siddha, and Yoga systems of medicine are of Indian origin. Ayurveda means knowledge of life. Its origin can be traced back to 5000 B.C (Vedic times). The medical knowledge in the Atharvaveda eventually developed into Ayurveda.
The Unani system is of Greek origin.

questions.stem: Samuel Hahnemann is referred to as the founding father of:
questions.explanation:
Samuel Hahnemann is the founding father of homeopathy. He was German. There are 3 principles in homeopathy:
Similia similibus curentur or human drug pathogenicity study: Treatment of disease using small amounts of drug that, in healthy people, would produce similar symptoms of the disease itself.
A single medicine is used for the treatment.
The minimum dose of the drug should be used.

questions.stem: The Tridosha theory of disease explains disease as a disturbance in the equilibrium of the three humors. To which system of medicine does this theory belong to?
questions.explanation:
Tridosha theory of disease belongs to Ayurveda. It explains disease as a disturbance in the equilibrium of the three humors, namely:
Vata (wind)
13
Pitta (gall)
Kapha (mucus).
A healthy person has a perfect balance of these humors.
This theory is similar to the Unani-tibb system of medicine which is based on four humors.

questions.stem: Which system of medicine originated in Tamil–speaking areas in south India?
questions.explanation:
The Siddha system of medicine originated from Tamil culture. It means achievement.
This system believes that sociodemographic, psychological, and physiological factors related to a person must be taken into account while deciding the medical treatment. They believe that disease is a disturbance in the equilibrium of three humors called vaadham, pittam, and kapham.

questions.stem: Where did the Unani–Tibb system of medicine originate?
questions.explanation:
The Unani-Tibb system of medicine originated in ancient Greece.
The Greeks believed that matter was made up of four elements. These elements had certain qualities that were represented in the body by the 4 humors and also determined the person's temperament.
Eleme nts | Qualiti es | Humors | Tempera ment
Earth | Cold | Phlegm | Phlegmat ic
Air | Dry | Yellow bi le | Choleric
Fire | Hot | Blood | Sanguine
Water | Moist | Black bil e | Melanch olic

questions.stem: Inoculating a person with a small amount of infective material to obtain protection against it was first pioneered by:
questions.explanation:
The procedure described is immunization. It was first pioneered in ancient Chinese medicine. They practiced variolation to prevent smallpox.
Note: Edward Jenner discovered the smallpox vaccine in 1796, the first vaccine to be discovered. He also coined the term vaccination.

questions.stem: Who is known as the first true epidemiologist in the history of medicine?
questions.explanation:
Hippocrates is known as the first true epidemiologist in the history of medicine. He is also known as the father of medicine.
He introduced the concept of the relationship between the environment and human health. He was the author of Airs, Water, and Places, a treatise on social medicine and hygiene as well as the Corpus Hippocraticum, a collection of 72 volumes of clinical case histories.
He also developed the Hippocratic Oath, which is considered the keystone of medical ethics.

questions.stem: Who was the architect of the Public Health Act of 1848?
questions.explanation:
Edwin Chadwick was the architect of the Public Health Act of 1848.
He was an English lawyer during the 1832 cholera epidemic. He compiled a report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population in Great Britain that eventually led to the passing of this act. It is considered a landmark act in the history of public health.

questions.stem: Identify the scientist who showed that anthrax was caused by a bacteria.
questions.explanation:
Robert Koch discovered that anthrax was caused by bacteria.
He also discovered the causative agents of tuberculosis and cholera. He won the Nobel prize in Physiology in 1905.
He also proposed Koch's postulates linking specific microorganisms to specific diseases. They state that the microorganism must be:
Found in abundance in diseased organisms, but not in healthy organisms.
Isolated from a diseased organism and grown in pure culture
Able to cause disease when inoculated into a healthy organism
Re-isolated from the diseased experimental host and identical to the original specific causative agent

questions.stem: In 1902, it was discovered that malaria was transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito. Who was behind this discovery?
questions.explanation:
Ronald Ross showed that malaria was transmitted by Anopheles mosquito. Option B: Charles Alphonse Laveran discovered the malarial parasite.
Option C: Walter Reed showed that yellow fever transmitted by Aedes mosquito.
Option D: David Bruce showed that African sleeping sickness/trypanosomiasis transmitted by the tsetse fly.

questions.stem: The first bacterium discovered as a cause of the disease was:
questions.explanation:
24
The first bacterium discovered as a cause of the disease is leprosy bacillus.
In 1873, Armauer Hansen demonstrated Mycobacterium leprae (rod-like bodies) from a leprosy nodule. This is the first time that chronic infectious disease in humans was shown to be related to a bacillus.
In 1876, Robert Koch validated the germ theory of disease after discovering the anthrax bacillus as the cause of anthrax.

questions.stem: Max Joseph von Pettenkofer described the concept of:
questions.explanation:
Pettenkofer of Munich put forth the theory of multifactorial causation of disease. Other theories of causation of disease include:
Spontaneous generation theory - given by Aristotle
Web of causation theory - given by MacMahon and Pugh
Supernatural theory of disease

questions.stem: In which country was the last case of naturally occurring smallpox in the world recorded?
questions.explanation:
The last case of naturally occurring smallpox was in Somalia in 1977.
The last case of smallpox occurred in 1978 when a medical photographer was accidentally exposed to the smallpox virus in a research laboratory in Birmingham.
India was declared smallpox-free on 24th May 1975. WHO declared smallpox as eradicated globally on 8th May 1980.

questions.stem: Who first coined the term social medicine?
questions.explanation:
Jules Guérin coined this term as editor of the Gazette médicale de Paris. He was a French orthopaedist in the mid-1800s.
Option A: John Ryle promoted social medicine in England in the early 1900s.
Option C: Alfred Grotjahn described social pathology, the social factors influencing diseases.
Option D: Francis Albert Eley Crew stated that social medicine stood on the pillars of medicine and sociology.

questions.stem: How would you define socialized medicine?
options: Subsidized medical care at government's expense
Free medical care provided and regulated by government alone
Free medical care at government expense, regulated by professional groups
Integration of social medicine with health care
questions.explanation:
Socialized medicine is the provision of medical service at the government's expense but is operated and regulated by professional groups, and not the government. Russia was the first
country to completely socialize medicine.
Free medical care by a government alone is called state medicine.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about socialized medicine except:
options: Ensures social equity and universal coverage
Use state funds for free medicine
questions.explanation:
Increasing the utilization of health services is not a component of socialized medicine.
It refers to the provision of medical service through the state funds; however, it is operated and regulated by professional groups. Russia was the first to completely socialize medicine.
It eliminates competition among physicians as well as ensures social equity and universal health coverage.

questions.stem: Who said that the secret of national health lies in the homes of people?
questions.explanation:
Florence Nightingale said that the secret of national health lies in the homes of people. She is considered the the founder of modern nursing.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following is not included in the WHO definition of health?
questions.explanation:
According to the WHO, health is “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity”.
In recent years, the definition has been modified to also include the ability to lead a “socially and economically productive life.”

questions.stem: Which of the following is the biomedical concept of disease based upon?
options: Combination of social, economic and political influences
questions.explanation:
The biomedical concept of disease is based on the germ theory of disease, which was postulated by Louis Pasteur.
The germ theory of disease states that microorganisms known as pathogens or germs can lead to disease. It was criticized that it did not include environmental, social, psychological, and cultural determinants of health.
The ecological concept of disease states that disease is the maladjustment of the human organism to the environment.
The psychosocial concept of disease hypothesised that health is also influenced by social, psychological, cultural and economic factors as well.
The holistic concept of disease includes all the above concepts to describe health.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a mortality indicator?
questions.explanation:
Life expectancy is a positive mortality indicator.
A set of values that measure the rate of mortality or death is known as mortality indicators.
Disability-adjusted life years (DALY), health adjusted life expectancy (HALE), and Sullivan’s Index are disability rates.

questions.stem: An epidemiologist is tasked with measuring the overall health status of a community using a morbidity indicator. Which of the following indicators will she not use?
options: Number of days of restricted activity
questions.explanation:
Number of days of restricted activity is a disability indicator.
Morbidity is defined as public health outcomes focusing on diseases, traumas, or injury. Morbidity indicators can be used to measure the overall health and extent of healthcare utilisation in a given population.
Disability is defined as public health outcomes related to health conditions that include limitations in personal activities and societal participation. There are two types of disability indicators as follows:
Event type indicators-
Number of days of restricted activity
Bed disability days
Work loss days (or school loss days) within a specified period
Person type indicators-
Limitation of mobility: e.g confined to bed
Limitation of activity: e.g limitation to perform the basic activities of daily living such as eating and going to the toilet

questions.stem: Which of the following indicators can be used to estimate the number of years a newborn would be expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality?
questions.explanation:
HALE (Health Adjusted Life Expectancy) is an indicator that can be used to estimate the number of years a newborn is expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality.
HALE is calculated using the life expectancy at birth with an adjustment for time spent in poor health. It captures both fatal and non-fatal health outcomes of average levels of population health. It is also sensitive to changes over time or differences between countries in the distribution of health states.
Sullivan's index is also known as disability-free life expectancy (DFLE) or active life expectancy. It is the average number of years an individual is expected to live free of disability if the current patterns of mortality and disability continue to apply. It doesn’t take into account premature death. As HALE includes not just disability but the larger definition of poor health, it is a better option with respect to the question.

questions.stem: While assessing the health needs of a community, an epidemiologist is tasked with estimating the burden of cholera in the area. Which of the following is the simplest measure he can use?
questions.explanation:
The proportional mortality rate is the simplest measure of estimating the burden of disease in the community. It signifies the proportion of all deaths that can be attributed to the disease.
It is calculated as follows:
Proportional mortality rate of a disease = (No. of deaths due to that disease in the year/ Total no. of deaths in the year) *100.
Option A: Case fatality rate measures the risk of persons dying from a certain disease within a given time period. It measures the killing power of a disease. It is used to link mortality to morbidity.
Option B: Incidence measures the rate at which new cases are occurring in a population. It is not influenced by the duration of the disease. The use of incidence is generally restricted to acute diseases.
Option C: Crude death rate is considered a fair indicator of the comparative health of the people. It is the rate of total deaths in a year compared to the mid-year population.

questions.stem: You are researching the overall burden of COVID on a given population. Which of the following disability indicators is the best measure of this?
questions.explanation:
Disability adjusted life years (DALY) is the best measure of the overall burden of a disease in a defined population. It is also the best measure of the effectiveness of interventions.
DALY is calculated as - Years of lost life prematurely (YLL) + Years lost to disability (YLD). It can measure both mortality and disability together.
As DALY is affected by premature loss of life, conditions that affect younger individuals like road traffic accidents have a high DALY. In comparison to this, Alzheimer's disease has a lower DALY as it is a disease that mostly develops during old age and so has a lower YLL.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a health utilisation rate?
options: Average length of stay in hospital
questions.explanation:
Bed disability days is not a utilisation rate. It is an event-type disability indicator. It is defined as the number of days a person spent in a hospital bed due to illness or injury.
Health utilisation rate is defined as the number of people making use of the available health services to the total number of individuals in that population.
Health utilisation rates include:
Proportion of infants immunized against 9 diseases in the expanded program on immunization
(EPI)
Proportion of women receiving antenatal care and supervised delivery
Percentage of population using family planning methods
Bed occupancy rate
Average length of stay in the hospital
Bed turnover ratio

questions.stem: As the medical superintendent of a hospital, you wish to optimise the utilization of health services. What bed turnover interval should you aim for?
questions.explanation:
For optimum utilization of health services in a hospital, bed turnover interval must always be slightly positive.
Bed turnover interval is defined as the time interval where a hospital bed is
left unoccupied following a patient’s discharge till the next patient occupies it after admission.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best indicator of availability, utilization, and effectiveness of health services?
questions.explanation:
Infant mortality rate (IMR) is the best indicator of the availability, utilization, and effectiveness of health care. It is a very sensitive indicator.
Infant mortality rate (IMR)= Number of deaths in the first year of life/Number of live births x 1000
It is also one of the best indicators of state failure. It is the most universally accepted health status indicator of the whole population and of the socio-economic status in which they live.
Note: The best indicator of socio-economic development is the under-5 mortality rate.

questions.stem: While reviewing a national health programme, you are asked to assess the cost-effectiveness of the interventions provided under it. Which indicator will you use to measure this?
questions.explanation: QALY(Quality Adjusted Life Years) is used in assessing the cost-effectiveness (value of money) of a medical intervention. It is a measure of both the quality and quantity of life lived. It indicates the number of years of life that would be added by the intervention.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a socio-economic determinant of health?
questions.explanation:
Lifestyle is a behavioural and socio-cultural determinant of health. It is not a socio-economic determinant.
Socio-economic determinants of health are the following:
Economic status (per capita GNP)
Education
Occupation
Political system
Lifestyle is simply the way people live. It reflects our social values, attitudes, and activities. It is composed of:
Cultural patterns (daily nutrition, superstitions)
Behavioral patterns (personal hygiene, sedentary life)
Lifelong personal habits (e.g. smoking, alcoholism)
Lifestyle is learned by social interaction with parents, siblings, friends, school, and mass media.
Our political system determines our health. It can help shape community health services with regards to resource allocation, manpower policy, choice of technology, and the degree to which these services are made available & accessible to all segments of the society.
The percentage of GDP spent on health is an indicator of political commitment. WHO recommends at least 5% of GDP to be spent on health care. India spends about 2.1 % of its GDP on health(budget 2022-23).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a socio-economic indicator of health?
questions.explanation:
Annual family income is not a socioeconomic indicator of health. Socio-economic indicators of health (mnemonic: H – FLAGGED):
Housing (number of persons per room)
Family size
Literacy rate (especially female literacy rate)
Availability of per capita calorie
GNP per capita
Growth rate of population
UnEmployment level
Dependency ratio

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false regarding positive health in today’s world?
options: It is dependent on social, economic, and cultural determinants
It is a mirage because of changing environment
It means that the body and mind are at peace
It includes provision of free health camps by the government
questions.explanation:
The provision of free health camps by the government is a concept of state medicine.
Health does not merely mean the absence of disease or provision of diagnostic, curative, and preventive services. It is a state of physical, mental, and social well-being.
The state of positive health is based on the idea of perfect functioning of the body and mind. According to this concept, health is:
Biologically a state in which every cell and organ in the body is functioning at optimum capacity
Psychologically a state in which the individual feels a sense of perfect well-being and mastery over his environment
Socially a state in which the individual's capacities for participation in the social system are optimal
This concept is too idealistic and can never become a reality. Humans can never be so perfectly adapted to the environment because everything in our life is subject to change.
As the goal of positive health is unattainable, a broader concept of improving the quality of life has emerged. This highlights that positive health depends on medical action and also on economic, cultural, and social factors in the community.

questions.stem: As per the WHO, which of the following is not included in the standard of living?
questions.explanation:
Social security is a component of the level of living as per the United Nations and not standard of living.
According to the WHO, the standard of living includes:
Income and occupation
Standards of housing, sanitation, and nutrition
Level of provision of health, educational, and recreational services It depends on per capita GNP.

questions.stem: Which of the following are components of the physical quality of life index (PQLI)?
questions.explanation: Infant mortality rate, literacy rate, and life expectancy at 1 year of age are the components of the physical quality of life index (PQLI).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best measure of the standard of living?
questions.explanation: Human development index (HDI) is the best measure of the standard of living of a population. Physical quality of life index (PQLI) measures the quality of life.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a component of the human development index (HDI)?
questions.explanation:
Infant mortality rate (IMR) is not a component of HDI. It is a component of the physical quality of life index (PQLI).
The human development index (HDI) is used to compare living standards in different countries. It includes the following dimensions or components:
Each dimension index is calculated using the formula: Dimension Index = (Actual Value -
Minimum Value)/(Maximum Value - Minimum Value)
HDI is the geometric mean of the three indices: ILife1/3 x	IEducation1/3	x	IIncome1/3.
As per the Human Development Report 2023-2024, India's Human Development Index (HDI)
value is 0.644. This places India at 134th out of 193 countries.
Compo nent | Indicator | Index
Longev ity | Life expectancy at birth | Life expectancy index
Knowl edge | Literacy and enrolment | Education index
Incom e | GNI per capita US$ (purchasi ng power parity-PPP) | GNI index(income ind ex)

questions.stem: What are the minimum and maximum values established for the calculation of the life expectancy index in HDI?
questions.explanation:
The minimum value established for the calculation of the life expectancy index in HDI is 20 years and the maximum is 85 years.
These minimum and maximum values are used to calculate the dimension indices in HDI and are called goalposts.
Each dimension index is calculated using the formula:
Dimension Index = (Actual Value - Minimum Value)/(Maximum Value - Minimum Value).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true regarding the education index used for calculating the HDI?
options: It includes expected years of schooling
Adult literacy rate is not considered
Minimum and maximum values are based on global data
questions.explanation:
The gross enrollment ratio is no longer used in obtaining the education index in HDI. It was used as an indicator earlier.
The education index is calculated by taking into account the mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling. Maximum and minimum values are based on global data.
Adult literacy rate and gross enrollment ratio were used as indicators before 2009.

questions.stem: Which of the following indices measures the deprivation in basic dimensions of the country in human development?
questions.explanation:

questions.stem: Which of the following is not included in the Ottawa charter for health promotion?
questions.explanation:
Building social security is not included in the Ottawa charter for health promotion.
The first international conference for health promotion was held in Ottawa on 21st Nov 1986. It produced a charter known as the Ottawa charter.
The charter identified five key action areas as given below:
Build healthy public policy
Create supportive environment for health
Strengthen community action for health
Develop personal skills
Reorient health services
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a component of the epidemiological triad for tuberculosis?
questions.explanation:
Duration of illness is not a part of the epidemiological triad for tuberculosis. The epidemiological triad includes host, agent and environment:
Host factors: Age, sex, religion, race, genetic profile, immune system
Agent factors:
Biological - bacteria, viruses
Chemical - poisons, alcohol, smoke
Physical - trauma, fire, radiation
Nutrition - lack/excess
Environmental factors:
Temperature, humidity, altitude
Water, milk, food
Radiation, pollution, noise
Crowding, housing, neighborhood
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
Hence, a malnourished child (host), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (agent) and overcrowding
(environment) form the epidemiological triad for tuberculosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most logical sequence?
questions.explanation:
Disease  Impairment  Disability  Handicap is the most logical sequence among the given options.
Disease is a state of physiological/psychological dysfunction. Impairment is any loss or abnormality in normal structure or function. Disability is the inability to carry out normal actions due to impairment.
Handicap is the disadvantage due to disability that limits fulfilment of a role that is normal.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: A salesman met with an unfortunate accident that led to him eventually losing his left foot. He has been unable to walk after this incident and so been rendered unemployed. Match the following examples with the corresponding events explaining the concept of disability.
questions.explanation:
The correctly matched events relating to the given example are as follows:
The WHO definition of impairment is "any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological or anatomical structure or function". E.g., loss of a foot. An initial impairment may cause a secondary impairment as well.
The WHO defines disability as ''any restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in the manner or within the range considered normal for a human being". Because of impairment, the affected person may be unable to carry out certain activities and hence the person is considered disabled.
According to the WHO, a handicap is "a disadvantage for a given individual, resulting from an impairment or a disability, that limits or prevents the fulfilment of a role that is normal (depending on age, sex, and social and cultural factors) for that individual". The disadvantages experienced by a person as a result of disability makes them handicapped.
Event | Example
Disease/Disord er | Accident
Impairment | Loss of fo ot
Disability | Cannot W alk
Handicap | Unemploy ed

questions.stem: Which of the following is most appropriate about the web of disease causation?
options: It implies that individual factors in the web have equal weightage
It implies that all the chains of causation must be controlled to prevent disease
It is mostly applicable for acute and rare diseases
It suggests ways of interrupting the disease occurrence
questions.explanation:
The web of causation for a disease suggests a number of ways to interrupt the disease occurrence/progression.
This model was suggested by MacMahon and Pugh in their book ‘Epidemiologic Principles and Methods’.
Web of causation considers all the predisposing factors and their complex interrelationship with each other. This model is ideally suited in the study of chronic disease. The web of causation does not imply that the disease is controlled only when all the multiple chains of causation are removed. Sometimes removal of one significant link is sufficient to control the disease.
In a multifactorial event, individual factors are by no means of equal weightage. The importance of each factor is expressed in terms of relative risk.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true regarding the pathogenesis period of a disease?
options: Recovery is seen in this period
Entry of causative agent is seen
questions.explanation:
Primary prevention is not possible in the pathogenesis period of a disease. It can only be done in the period of pre-pathogenesis.
The two phases in the natural history of a disease include:
Period of pre-pathogenesis: It is before the onset of disease in humans. The disease agent has not entered the host, but the factors favouring the disease already exist. Primary
prevention (health promotion and specific protection) is applicable in this period.
Period of pathogenesis: It begins with the entry of the organism till recovery, death or disability. Secondary (halting of the disease process) and tertiary prevention (measures to limit disability) are applicable in this period. It isn't always characterised by the presence of disease symptoms as it also includes subclinical cases.

questions.stem: In the iceberg phenomenon of disease, which of the following does not represent the submerged portion of the iceberg?
questions.explanation:
Epidemiologically, the iceberg phenomenon of disease, diagnosed cases are represented by the floating tip of the iceberg.
The iceberg phenomenon of disease is related to the spectrum of disease. The water surface is the line of demarcation between the apparent and inapparent infections.
The submerged portion of the iceberg represents the hidden mass of diseases like asymptomatic, latent, and undiagnosed cases. Screening is done to identify these cases.
The iceberg phenomenon of disease is depicted in the image below.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases shows the iceberg phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Rubella shows the iceberg phenomenon of disease.
The iceberg phenomenon of diseases is not shown by diseases such as tetanus, rabies, and measles.
Iceberg phenomenon is shown by:
Polio
Influenza
Rubella
Mumps
Japanese Encephalitis
Diphtheria
Hepatitis A and B
Tuberculosis
Diabetes
Malnutrition
Hypertension
Note: If a disease has more number of subclinical infections, it shows the iceberg phenomenon of disease depicted in the image below.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: What is the term used to describe the interruption in the transmission of a disease?
questions.explanation:
Interruption in the transmission of a disease is called elimination. It is a step towards eradication.
Elimination is a reduction in the number of new cases of an infectious disease to zero (or a very low defined target rate) in a defined geographical area as a result of deliberate efforts. Continued measures to prevent re-establishment of transmission are required.
Eradication is a complete and permanent worldwide reduction to zero new cases of an infectious disease through deliberate efforts. No further control measures are required.
Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and ill health.
Control aims at decreasing the incidence, duration and transmission of the disease. It also aims at decreasing the physical and psychological complications of a disease.

questions.stem: Among the following options, which aids the most in disease elimination?
questions.explanation:
Herd immunity aids the most in disease elimination.
Herd immunity achieved, especially through immunization, goes a long way in helping the elimination of diseases. When a high level of herd immunity is maintained, the susceptible population is reduced to a small proportion, thereby eliminating the disease.
The purpose of isolation is to protect the community by preventing the transfer of infection from the reservoir to the possible susceptible hosts. Quarantine refers to restrictions on the healthy contacts of an infectious disease.

questions.stem: While collecting surveillance data for disease X, you find that the incidence of the disease is zero in your region. Which of the following statements best describes this scenario?
options: Disease is eliminated from the region.
Disease is well controlled in the region.
Disease is eradicated from the region.
Disease shows iceberg phenomenon in the region.
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, as the disease has zero incidence, we can say the disease has been eliminated from the region.
Elimination is a reduction in the number of new cases of an infectious disease to zero (or a very low defined target rate) in a defined geographical area as a result of deliberate efforts. Continued measures to prevent re-establishment of transmission are required.
Eradication is a complete and permanent worldwide reduction to zero new cases of an infectious disease through deliberate efforts. No further control measures are required.
Control aims at decreasing the incidence, duration and transmission of the disease. It also aims at decreasing the physical and psychological complications of a disease.
The iceberg phenomenon of disease is related to the spectrum of disease. The submerged portion of the iceberg represents the hidden mass of diseases like asymptomatic, latent, and undiagnosed cases. The clinical or diagnosed cases are represented by the floating tip of the iceberg and not the submerged portion. As disease incidence is zero here, there are no cases to form the iceberg.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a silent epidemic?
questions.explanation:
Alzheimer’s disease is referred to as the silent epidemic of the century.
Nearly 50 million people globally are living with this disease. Since it strikes so often, so arbitrarily, and with such little warning, many have dubbed it the silent epidemic.

questions.stem: What is the analysis of routine measurements aimed at detecting changes in the health status of a population called?
questions.explanation:
The analysis of routine measurements aimed at detecting changes in the health status or environment of a population is called monitoring.
Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and ill health.
Sentinel surveillance is a method of identifying the missing cases and thereby supplementing the notified cases.
Systematic reviews involve a detailed plan with the goal of reducing bias by identifying, appraising, and synthesizing all relevant studies on a particular topic.

questions.stem: In which of the following does surveillance of disease not have a direct role?
options: Data on new and changing trends
questions.explanation:
Surveillance of a disease does not have a direct role in breaking the chain of transmission.
Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and ill health.
It helps in health planning and provides information about public health disasters including data on new and changing trends of disease.
Surveillance requires professional analysis and sophisticated judgment of data, leading to recommendations for control activities.

questions.stem: Measures in sentinel surveillance do not aim at identifying:
questions.explanation:
Sentinel surveillance does not include identifying cases free of disability.
Sentinel surveillance helps in identifying the missing cases, in addition to the already existing and new cases. It is used for supplementing routine notifications.

questions.stem: Which of the following is public health surveillance preferentially aimed at?
questions.explanation:
Public health surveillance is preferentially aimed at health planning.
Public health surveillance provides important feedback on the health status of the population, about planning control and prevention activities, and also for public health disasters.

questions.stem: Which of the following is included under primordial prevention of coronary artery disease?
questions.explanation:
Adoption of a healthy lifestyle from childhood would fall under the category of primordial prevention of coronary artery disease.
Primordial prevention is preventing the emergence of risk factors among population groups in which these risk factors have not yet appeared. Most adult health problems (obesity, hypertension) have their early origins in childhood. It is in childhood that lifestyles are formed i.e. eating patterns, physical exercise, smoking, etc.
In primordial prevention, efforts are made to discourage children from adopting harmful lifestyles.
These lifestyle changes when made by adults are known as primary prevention.

questions.stem: What type of prevention is the prescriptive screening of a disease?
questions.explanation:
Prescriptive screening of a disease is an example of secondary prevention.
Prescriptive screening of disease can lead to early diagnosis of disease. By early diagnosis, intervention can be made to prevent disability. Hence, it comes under secondary prevention.

questions.stem: What form of prevention is prospective screening?
questions.explanation:
Prospective screening is a type of primary prevention.
Prospective screening is done on healthy individuals to screen for disease. It is done prior to the onset of the disease. E.g., screening donated blood for HIV before it is transfused. This type of prevention reduces the incidence of disease.
Note: Prescriptive screening is done for case detection. People are screened for their own benefits. It is an early diagnosis of diseases existing in them. This is a form of secondary prevention. E.g., neonatal screening for hypothyroidism, pap smear for detection of cervical cancer.

questions.stem: You advise a reproductive age woman to vaccinate against HPV. What is this type of prevention called?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario of immunisation is an example of primary prevention.
Primary prevention is an action taken before the onset of disease. This reduces the possibility of disease occurrence. Hence, immunization is a form of primary prevention, through specific protection.
Examples of primary prevention include immunization, sanitation, solid and liquid waste management etc.

questions.stem: Who among the following is not a target for primary prevention?
questions.explanation:
Asymptomatic patients are the target population for secondary prevention but not for primary prevention.
Primary prevention is implemented before the onset of the disease. Hence, all patients including asymptomatic ones are not included in the target group.

questions.stem: As a part of the iodine deficiency control programme, you advocate the usage of iodized salt in hilly areas. What is this type of prevention an example of?
questions.explanation: The usage of iodized salt in iodine-deficient areas like in hilly regions is an example of primary prevention as it provides specific protection.

questions.stem: You are performing a routine pap smear on a 30-year-old woman in the gynecology OPD. What level of prevention does this fall under?
questions.explanation:
Pap smear is a screening test for carcinoma cervix and is an example of secondary prevention.
Early diagnosis (including screening) and treatment are the components of secondary prevention. Some of the examples of secondary prevention are as follows:
Papanicolaou (Pap) smear for early detection of cervical cancer
Mammography for early detection of breast cancer
Colonoscopies for early detection of colon cancer
Blood Pressure Screening
Secondary prevention measures focus on the sub-clinical stage and the early clinical stage, such as dysplasia in this case.
These measures enable early detection and prompt effective intervention to correct departures from a state of health.

questions.stem: What mode of prevention is disability prevention by appropriate treatment an example of?
questions.explanation:
Disability prevention by appropriate treatment is an example of secondary prevention. This is because disability has not occurred yet so correct treatment can stop it from developing.
After the disability has set in, prevention of progression of disability from transitioning into a handicap is tertiary prevention. It is also called disability limitation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of disability limitation?
options: Starting a patient on anti-tuberculous therapy
questions.explanation:
Prescribing spectacles for refractive error is an example of disability limitation which is a component of tertiary prevention. This mode of intervention is applicable when the patient presents late in the pathogenesis phase.
The objective of this intervention is to prevent or halt the transition of the disease process from impairment to handicap.
Option B: Starting a patient on anti-tuberculous therapy is secondary prevention as it is a part of treatment.
Option C: Abstinence from smoking is a modification of the risk factor. Hence it is an example of primary prevention.
Option D: Early fixation of fractures will prevent disability. Hence, it is an example of secondary prevention.

questions.stem: Which among the following diseases was eliminated in India in 2015?
questions.explanation:
Maternal and neonatal tetanus was eliminated from India in 2015, as certified by the WHO. Important years for India (declared disease-free):
Infective trachoma - 2017
Yaws - 2016
Maternal & neonatal tetanus - 2015
Polio - 2014
Guinea worm disease (dracunculiasis) - 2000 Worldwide eradication:
Type-2 wild poliovirus - 2015
Type-3 wild poliovirus- 201š
Smallpox - 1š›0

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about ICD- 11?
options: It includes a new chapter on traditional medicine
Gender incongruence is now listed as part of mental health
The codes relating to antimicrobial resistance are more closely in line with the Global Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System
It has come into full effect from January 2022
questions.explanation:
The new ICD-11 has a new chapter on sexual health that contains gender incongruence, which was previously listed under mental health conditions in the ICD-10.
The ICD 11 was released by the WHO in June 201› and was presented at the World Health Assembly in May 201š for adoption by the Member States. It has come into effect from 1 January 2022.
Its designations for antibiotic resistance align with the Global Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System (GLASS). It is given by the WHO and is revised every 10 years.
New chapters added in ICD-11 are:
Traditional medicine
Sexual health: Gender incongruence has been moved from mental health to sexual health.
Gaming disorder has been added under Addictive disorders.
Immune system disorders, which will enable the better study of allergies.
It has more detail on cancer, specifically different types of skin cancer, as well as on heart health and weight disorders compared to ICD-10.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not included in the format of the death certificate recommended by the WHO?
options: Other significant conditions contributing to death
Age of person at the time of death
questions.explanation: Age at the time of death is not included in the WHO format for a death certificate.

questions.stem: You are filling the death certificate of a patient who died from rupture of the myocardium following an acute myocardial infarction. This was because of thrombosis in the coronary artery due to longstanding atherosclerosis. What will you record in line I (c) of the death certificate?
questions.explanation:
Coronary artery thrombosis is to be filled in line I (c) of the death certificate as one of the antecedent causes in the order of the events that took place.
The flow of events in this patient is as follows:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
As per the recommendations of Forty-Third World Health Assembly 1990, an additional line (d)
was added below (c) in part I of the death certificate, as approved by the WHO.
Part II will only be filled up with a significant condition contributing to the death but not related to the disease or condition causing it.

questions.stem: An HIV positive patient was suffering from multi-drug resistant tuberculosis. He died of respiratory failure due to lobar pneumonia. Which of the following options is the most appropriate for the line I (a) of the death certificate?
questions.explanation:
Lobar pneumonia is appropriate for line I (a) of the death certificate. Line I (a) consists of the immediate cause of death such as the disease/condition. Immediate cause is the immediate/terminal event leading to death
In this patient:
I(a) - Disease directly leading to death: Lobar pneumonia
I(b) - Antecedent cause: MDR tuberculosis.
II- HIV
Respiratory failure is a mode of dying in this patient. It is not the cause of death.
Terminal events like circulatory failure and respiratory failure, are modes of dying. They should not be written as the immediate cause of death in the death certificate because they are just signs of death.
Simply put, respiratory failure is 'how he died' whereas lobar pneumonia is 'why he died'. Therefore, lobar pneumonia (why he died) is the cause of the death.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a morbidity indicator?
questions.explanation:
Years of potential life lost is not a morbidity indicator. It is a mortality indicator. It is the years of potential life lost through premature death.
Notification rates, spells of sickness and incidence are examples of morbidity indicators.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about rate is false?
options: It measures the occurrence of an event in a population.
It has no specification of time.
It's numerator is mostly part of the denominator.
questions.explanation:
Rate is the measurement of the occurrence of a particular event in a given time. Hence, rates have a specification in time.
Examples include crude death rate, incidence rate etc.

questions.stem: To calculate the crude death rate of a country, at what time of the year is the population assessed?
questions.explanation:
The crude death rate is a mortality indicator, which uses the mid-year population as its denominator. The mid-year population is always attributed as the population on 1st July of any year.
Hence for calculating the crude death rate, the population is assessed on the 1st of July.

questions.stem: For which of the following purposes is age-specific death rates not used?
options: Identifying specific age groups at risk
Comparison for different causes within the same population
Comparison between different sexes in relation to accidents
Comparison between different age groups in relation to accidents
questions.explanation:
Sex-specific death rates are used for the comparison between sexes and not age-specific death rates.
Age-specific death rates are used for:
Comparison for different causes within the same population.
Comparison between different age groups in relation to a particular event.
Identifying specific age groups at risk.

questions.stem: An epidemiologist is assessing an outbreak of acute diarrhoeal disease in a region. He wants to predict the virulence of the causative agent. Which of the following parameters will he use for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Case fatality rate is used in this scenario as it is the most useful parameter to predict the virulence of an acute illness. It represents the killing power of disease.
Note:
Case fatality rate is an incidence proportion and not a true rate as no time interval is used for its calculation.

questions.stem: Case fatality rate is .
options: ‹illing power of a disease in time
‹illing power of a disease with no time interval
questions.explanation: Case fatality rate reflects the killing power of a disease with no specific time interval.

questions.stem: A village has a population of 30,000 people. 500 of them contracted a disease X, out of which 75 died. What is the case fatality rate?
questions.explanation:
Case fatality rate is given by the formula:
[[IMG:1]]
The total number of cases of disease X= 500 The total number of deaths= 75
Hence the case fatality rate= 75/500 x 100 = 15%

questions.stem: In a village of 5000 people, an outbreak of cholera led to 200 cases with 50 deaths. What is the case fatality rate?
questions.explanation:
The case fatality rate is 25%.
Case fatality rate: (Total number of deaths due to a particular disease)/(Total number of cases due to the same disease)x 100
: 50/200 * 100 = 25%

questions.stem: Which of the following is the simplest measure of the burden of a disease in a community?
questions.explanation:
The proportional mortality rate is the simplest measure to estimate the burden of a disease in a community.
It is commonly used for broad disease groups and when population data is not available.It is of limited value in making comparisons between populations and in identifying risk groups.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Among the following, which measurement can be used as a yardstick for the assessment of standards of therapy?
questions.explanation:
The survival rate can be used as a yardstick for the assessment of standards of therapy. It is used as a method of describing prognosis and is widely employed in cancer studies. The survival rate is given by the following formula.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Standardisation was done before comparing the mortality rates of two countries. What is the rationale behind this?
options: Due to difference in number of deaths.
Due to difference in age distribution.
Due to difference in the population density.
Due to difference in cause of death.
questions.explanation:
While comparing the mortality rates of two countries, the standardization of rates is done due to differences in age distribution.
The two types of standardisation include direct and indirect.
In both methods, a standard population is chosen where the numbers in each age and sex group are known and its choice is arbitrary.
The commonly used standard populations are the Segi world population and the European standard population.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about the standardized mortality ratio?
options: It is a form of direct standardization.
Observed deaths and expected deaths are part of its formula.
It can be used if the event of interest is occurrence of disease.
questions.explanation: Standardized mortality ratio is a form of indirect standardization.

questions.stem: A party was attended by 110 people out of which, 40 did not eat fruit salad. Among the rest of those who ate fruit salad, 55 developed food poisoning. What is the attack rate?
questions.explanation:
The attack rate is calculated by the formula:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
In this scenario, the number of new cases is 55 and the total number of those at risk is 70 as they ate the fruit salad.
Therefore attack rate = 55/70 X 100 = 7‘.6%.
Attack rate is an incidence rate. It is used only when the population is exposed to risk for a limited period.

questions.stem: Out of a family of 4 members, one of them developed COVID-19 infection. Four days later, 2 other members developed the same. What is the secondary attack rate?
questions.explanation:
Secondary attack rate is calculated by the following:
In this scenario, there is one primary case. The total exposed contacts are the other 3 members of the family. The number of persons developing the disease is 2.
So, secondary attack rate = 2/3 x 100 = 66%.
Note: The primary case is excluded from both the numerator and denominator.

questions.stem: Which of the following study designs would you prefer for calculating the incidence of a disease?
questions.explanation: The study designs which can be used to calculate incidence are cohort studies and longitudinal studies.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about incidence are true?
questions.explanation:
Incidence is not affected by the duration of the disease. Analysis of incidence rates may provide useful insights into the effectiveness of the health services provided.
Incidence is the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a period of time. Prevalence is more than incidence as it is the product of incidence and duration.
Incidence is a type of rate and not a proportion.

questions.stem: A medical officer noticed that there were 300 new cases of cholera in an area in a year. The total population in that area is 30,000. What is the incidence of cholera?
questions.explanation:
The incidence of cholera is 10 per 1000. Incidence is given by the formula:
[[IMG:1]]
In this scenario number of new cases = 300 Total population = 30,000
Hence the incidence rate = (300/30,000) × 1000 = 10
Therefore it is 10 per 1000 per year.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a good indicator of efficacy of health programs?
questions.explanation: Incidence is a good indicator of the efficacy of health services and programs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false with regard to prevalence?
options: It is a product of incidence and duration.
It can be determined by a cross-sectional study.
It is an example of rate.
It is point prevalence unless specified.
questions.explanation:
Prevalence is a proportion, not a rate.
Prevalence is the proportion of all cases, old and new, of a particular disease at a given point in time or over a period of time in a given population. It can be determined from cross-sectional studies.
Types of prevalence:
Point prevalence is the prevalence at a point in time. Usually, prevalence is point prevalence unless otherwise specified.
Period prevalence is the prevalence over a period of time.

questions.stem: The incidence of a disease is 4 per 1000 of the population with an average duration of 2 years. What is the prevalence?
questions.explanation:
The prevelance in the given situation is ‘/1000 population. Prevalence is given by the formula :
Prevalance = Incidence x Mean Duration Prevalence = 4/1000 x 2 = ‘/1000 population

questions.stem: A village has a total population of 100,000 with an under-16 population at 3%. The prevalence of goitre in the under-16 population is (0.3/100). What is the total number of under-16 population affected by goitre?
questions.explanation:
The total number of persons in the under-16 with goitre is 9. Number of total under-16 population = 3% of 100,000 = 3000.
Thus, total number of goitre patients who are under-16 with the prevalence at the given value =
3000*0.3/100= 9

questions.stem: In a population of 5000, new cases of TB are 500 and old cases are 50. What is the prevalence of TB in this case?
questions.explanation:
Prevalence is given by the formula:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
In the given scenario total no.of cases :50(old)+ 500(new) =550.
Hence prevalence = (550/5000) x 100 = 11%

questions.stem: In a village having a population of 5000, a diagnostic test for a particular disease showed the following results. What is the prevalence of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Prevalence is given by the formula:
In this scenario, the number of cases: 1000+500 = 1500. Total population: 5000
Prevalence= 1500/5000 × 100 = 30%.

questions.stem: A randomized control trial showed an effective treatment against an infectious disease. It was then incorporated by the health system. Which of the following is subsequently expected to happen?
questions.explanation:
A new effective treatment for infectious disease would reduce the duration of the disease, thereby reducing prevalence.
Note: Both prevalence and incidence decrease but prevalence is the first to show a change in pattern. Hence, ‘prevalence decreases’ is the better answer.

questions.stem: There was an outbreak of hepatitis A infection in your town. Proper prevention strategies were enforced. What is expected to happen at first to the number of cases of hepatitis A?
questions.explanation: In the given scenario, prevention of hepatitis A would lead to decrease in incidence at first. Prevention of an acute disease would prevent new cases, thus first decreasing incidence.

questions.stem: A new drug was approved for the treatment of prostate cancer. It has been shown to prevent early deaths but not cure the cancer. What is expected to happen to the cases of prostate cancer over a period of time?
options: Increase in incidence, no change in prevalence
Decrease in incidence, increase in prevalence
Increase in incidence, decrease in prevalence
Increase in prevalence, no change in incidence
questions.explanation:
A new drug that prevents death yet does not cure the disease will cause an increase in prevalence but the incidence remains the same.
In the given scenario, the drug reduces early deaths but does not cure prostate cancer. Hence, there is a paradoxical increase in the prevalence while the incidence remains the same.
Prevalence depends on two factors, the incidence and duration of illness. If the population is stable and incidence and duration are unchanging, the relationship between incidence and prevalence can be expressed as:
P = I X D
(I - Incidence and D - Mean duration)
This equation shows longer the duration of the disease, the greater the prevalence. Note:
In chronic diseases like TB, prevalence will be higher than incidence.
If a new treatment for a disease is effective, incidence does not change but prevalence decreases as the duration of disease decreases.
If the treatment only prevents death but doesn’t cure the disease, it may cause a paradoxical increase in prevalence.

questions.stem: Cross product ratio can be arrived from:
questions.explanation: Cross product ratio (Odds ratio) can be obtained from the case-control study.

questions.stem: A person wants to study about the relationship between smoking and lung cancer, so he collects data about people diseased with lung cancer from government hospitals and the number of cigarette packets sold at the same time period. Which type of study is this?
questions.explanation:
The type of study described is an ecological study as the unit of study is the population. The number of cigarette packets sold at the same time is data about the population.
Option A: The unit of study in a cross-sectional study is an individual.
Option C: There is no experiment done here. Hence, it is not experimental study.
Option D: Quasi-experiments are nonrandomized, pre-post intervention studies done when it is not feasible or ethical to conduct a randomized controlled trial. The unit of study is therefore patients or individuals and not population.

questions.stem: A researcher is planning to study the etiology of certain painful idiopathic peripheral neuropathies. Which of the following study methods shall he choose?
questions.explanation: Diseases of unknown etiology or new diseases can be studied with descriptive epidemiology.

questions.stem: The preliminary observations made by Burkitt in Africa eventually found that the Epstein-Barr Virus is an etiological factor for Burkitt lymphoma. What is this study an example of?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is an example of a descriptive study.
Descriptive studies are used to describe a disease of unknown etiology. These studies also led to the discovery of prions as the etiological agents of chronic degenerative neurological disorders (Kuru) in humans. This is also an example of a descriptive study.
Types of epidemiological studies:
Observational studies - allow nature to take its own course, the investigator measures but does not intervene.
Descriptive studies - limited to the description of the occurrence of a disease in a population.
Analytical studies - go further by analyzing the relationship between health status and other variables.
Ecological studies
Cross-sectional studies
Case-control studies
Cohort studies
Experimental studies or intervention studies involve an active attempt to change a disease determinant or the progress of a disease and are similar in design to experiments in other sciences.
Randomized controlled trials
Field trials
Community trials

questions.stem: Which of the following are included in descriptive epidemiology?
questions.explanation: Descriptive epidemiology involves describing the disease in terms of time, place, and person distribution.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the term hypothesis?
questions.explanation:
An epidemiological hypothesis is a supposition or variable. It is arrived at from observation and needs to be tested.
Descriptive studies primarily focus on the formulation of a hypothesis.
Analytical studies which include study designs like case-control and cohort are used to test the formulated hypothesis. The hypothesis can subsequently be rejected or accepted.
Experimental studies involve an intervention to provide scientific proof for etiological risk factors of diseases and to measure the efficiency of health services.

questions.stem: The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases is planning to study the natural history of COVID-19. Which of the following studies can be used?
questions.explanation:
Longitudinal studies are useful to study the natural history of a disease.
It is also used to identify risk factors, and to find the incidence rate. In longitudinal studies, observations are repeated in the same population over a prolonged period of time by follow-up examinations. Their disadvantage is that they are difficult to organize and take a very long time.

questions.stem: What are prevalence studies also known as?
questions.explanation:
Cross-sectional studies help in obtaining the prevalence of a disease. Hence, they are also known as prevalence studies.
Cross-sectional study is a type of observational study where a cross-section of a population is examined once at one point in time. It is more useful in studying chronic diseases than acute ones. They do not provide information on the natural history of disease or incidence and also do not establish the time sequence.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about point source epidemic is false?
options: Clustering of cases occur within a short period of time
It occurs only due to an infectious agent
All cases usually develop within one incubation period
questions.explanation:
Point source epidemics are caused not only due to infectious agents but also by environmental pollution and contamination of food.
Point source epidemics belong to the common source type of epidemics. Exposure to disease agents is brief so they are also called single exposure epidemics.
All cases develop within one incubation period. In the epidemic curve, there is a sharp rise and fall as all cases are clustered within one incubation period. There are no secondary waves and these epidemics tend to be explosive.

questions.stem: Identify the type of epidemic depicted from the following epidemic curve. [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
Point-source epidemic is depicted in the given image.
In the epidemic curve for a point-source epidemic, there is a sharp rise and fall of the curve with no secondary waves. It tends to be explosive as all the cases are clustered in a narrow period of time. It occurs within one incubation period of the disease.

questions.stem: An outbreak of viral hepatitis A was reported from a town between June and September of a particular year. The peak of the outbreak occurred in July. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation:
This outbreak of viral hepatitis A is an example of a common source, multiple exposure type of epidemic.
The incubation period of hepatitis A is approximately 28 days (range 15 to 50 days). In this scenario, the cases of viral hepatitis A have occurred over a period from June to September (120 days) which is more than one incubation period of the disease. This is suggestive of multiple
exposures from a common source.
If the period of the outbreak falls within one incubation period, then the type of epidemic is common source ,single exposure or point source epidemic.
Difference between single exposure and multiple exposure epidemics:
Propagated epidemic results from person to person transmission of the infectious agent over a prolonged duration of time. For e.g. Polio epidemic, COVID-19.
Note: Hepatitis A epidemic is generally an example of a propagated epidemic. However, it does not always follow this pattern. In the given scenario, since the outbreak lasts for a short duration of 3 months (about 3 incubation periods for hepatitis A), it is considered to be a point source, multiple exposure outbreak.
 | Common source, single expo sure epidemic | Common source, multiple ex posure epidemic
Nature of exposure | Single, brief exposure | Multiple, continuous or inter mittent exposures for a prolo nged time
Nature of epidemic | Explosivewith clustering of c ases within a short interval of time | Less chance of clusteringof ca ses within short interval of ti me
Duration of epidem ic | Falls<1 incubation periodof a particular disease | Extends>1 incubation period of a particular disease
Example | An epidemic offood poisonin g | Outbreak ofcholera

questions.stem: The sales team of a corporate company presents to the hospital with complaints of sudden onset nausea, vomiting and loose stools. They give a history of having food from a nearby bakery three hours ago. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of food poisoning. It is a type of common-source (point-source),
single exposure epidemic.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of disease following a seasonal trend?
options: Occurrence of rubella every 6-9 years in the pre-vaccination era
Occurrence of influenza pandemic every 7-10 years
Occurrence of bacterial gastroenteritis in summer
Increase in the occurrence of diabetes in developed countries
questions.explanation:
Occurrence of bacterial gastroenteritis in summer is an example of a disease following seasonal trend.
Seasonal trend is a type of periodic fluctuation. It refers to the occurrence of a disease in seasonal variation influenced by environmental conditions like climate, rainfall, life cycle of vectors, heat, etc.
Examples are:
Measles and varicella in early spring
Bacterial gastroenteritis in summer
Heatstroke in summer
Dengue in July-November
Respiratory infections in winter.

questions.stem: The influenza pandemic is anticipated to occur every 7-10 years due to the antigenic variation of the virus. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation:
The influenza pandemic occuring every 7–10 years due to antigenic variations of the virus is an example of a disease showing cyclical trend.
Diseases occurring in cycles spread over a short period of time show cyclical trends of time distribution. Cyclical trend is a type of periodic fluctuation.
Examples include:
Measles: every 2-3 years in the pre-vaccination era.
Rubella: 6-9 years in the pre-vaccination era.
Non-infectious conditions can also show cyclical trends.

questions.stem: How often did the cyclical trends of measles occured in the pre-vaccination era?
questions.explanation: In the pre-vaccination era, the cyclical trends of measles occurred every 2-3 years, while that of rubella occurred every 6-9 years.

questions.stem: What is known as the change in the occurrence of a disease over very long periods of time?
questions.explanation:
A secular trend refers to the changes in the occurrence of a disease over long periods of time
(decade).
Usually, disease distributions tend to move in one particular direction over a period of time. Examples: Decrease in diseases like polio, tuberculosis, and typhoid fever, but increase in diabetes and coronary artery disease in developed countries.

questions.stem: Which of the following cannot be depicted by the image given below? [[IMG:1]]
options: Rural - urban distributions of a disease
questions.explanation:
The given image is of a spot map. Spot maps are not used to depict rural-urban distributions of a disease. They help to understand the local distributions of a disease.
They are also called shaded maps. This method was used by John Snow to investigate the epidemic of cholera in London in 1854. They depict areas of high or low frequency, the boundaries, and patterns of disease distribution.

questions.stem: What are migration studies used to evaluate?
options: Socio-demographic reasons for migration of a population
Prevalence of diseases in a population
Environmental and genetic factors of a disease in a population
Incidence of disease in the immigrant population
questions.explanation:
Migration studies are used to evaluate the role of genetic and environmental factors of a disease in a population.
The two methods used are:
Comparing disease and death rates of migrants with kin who stayed at home
Comparing disease and death rates of migrants with the local population of the host country Limitations of these studies:
Non-randomization of these groups
Environmental factors may act only up to a certain age
Not useful for diseases with long incubation periods

questions.stem: What does bimodality in person distribution refer to?
options: Description of two etiological hypotheses of a disease in one person
Evaluation of two different environmental factors of a person in disease causation
Two separate peaks in the age incidence curve of a disease
Equal incidence of a disease in male and female population
questions.explanation:
Bimodality refers to the occurence two separate peaks in the age incidence curve of a disease.
Example: Hodgkin's lymphoma shows a bimodal curve with peaks at 15–20 years and 70–80 years.
The image below shows bimodality in the age incidence curve:
