questions.stem: You are conducting a cohort study in a group of headload workers to identify the risk factors for developing low back pain in future. This type of study falls under which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Cohort studies fall under non-experimental (observational) analytical studies. Classification of epidemiological studies:
Observational studies: allow nature to take its own course, the investigator measures but does not intervene. It is further classified into:
Descriptive studies: limited to describing the occurrence of a disease in a population.
Analytical studies: go further by analyzing the relationship between health status and other variables. It includes:
Ecological studies
Cross-sectional studies
Case-control studies
Cohort studies
Experimental studies or interventional studies: it involves an active attempt to change a disease determinant or the progress of a disease, and is similar in design to experiments in other sciences.
Randomized controlled trials
Field trials
Community trials

questions.stem: What is the unit of observation in ecological studies?
questions.explanation:
In ecological studies, the unit of observation is the population or community.
Type of study | Unit
Ecological/ Correlational | Population
Cross-sectional/ Prevalence | Individual
Case-control/ Case reference | Individual
Cohort/ Follow up | Individual
Randomised Controlled Tria ls | Patients
Field Trial | Healthy peo ple
Type of study	Unit | Type of study	Unit
Community trial | Community

questions.stem: Identify the type of study from the following design: [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The design given is of a case-control study. It proceeds from effect to cause and is done after the exposure and outcome have occurred.
It tries to determine the possible exposure factors after a known disease incidence. This is the first approach to test causal hypotheses and uses controls to support or refute an inference.
Retrospective or historical cohort study, on the other hand, tries to compare the risk of developing a disease to some already known exposure factors. Ex: risk of lung cancer in uranium miners, risk of angiosarcoma in persons exposed to polyvinyl chloride etc.
Retrospective cohort studies are more economical and quicker than prospective cohort studies.

questions.stem: A study was conducted among a group of 500 patients with lung cancer and another group of 300 people chosen from the general population. Both the groups were questioned about their exposure to smoking. What kind of study is this?
questions.explanation:
This is a case-control study. In this scenario, 500 patients constitute the cases and 300
people from the general population constitute the controls. The study is done from effect (lung cancer) to cause (smoking).

questions.stem: A case-control study was conducted to evaluate the association between lifestyle risk factors and the prevalence of dyslipidemia. Which of the following is not an advantage of this type of study?
questions.explanation: Incidence cannot be calculated from case-control studies. Incidence can be calculated from cohort studies, also known as longitudinal studies.

questions.stem: A case-control study was conducted to see if symptoms of upper gastrointestinal dysfunction occurred more frequently in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Which of the following cannot be used as controls in this study?
questions.explanation:
Siblings cannot be used as controls while studying genetic conditions because the outcome would be distorted due to their similarities.
Controls in a case-control study:
Usually disease-free
Can be up to 4 times the number of cases in small studies
In large studies, a 1:1 ratio of cases and controls can be sought
Sources: general population, hospitals, relatives (spouses and siblings), neighbors, or colleagues
Although, siblings cannot be used as controls for studies on genetic conditions

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a cause of bias in a case-control study?
questions.explanation:
Hawthorne bias is not seen in case-control studies. This bias occurs when the subjects change their attitude/ actions while under observation. This distorts the results of the cohort or experimental studies.
The bias that are seen in the case-control study are:
Confounding
Recall bias
Selection bias
Berkesonian bias
Interviewer's bias

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about random errors?
options: Systematic errors are different from random errors
questions.explanation:
Random errors are not causes of bias.
Random error arises when a value of the sample measurement diverges, due to chance alone, from that of the true population value. They can never be completely eliminated.
Sources of random errors are individual biological variations, sampling errors, and measurement errors.
Systematic errors are also called biases. They are different from random errors.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors in a study will cause Berkesonian bias?
options: Interviewer asking leading questions to the subjects
Different rates of hospital admission of different diseases
Researcher's belief in the treatment changing the outcome of the study
Cases that are lost to follow-up
questions.explanation: Berkesonian bias occurs due to the different rates of hospital admission of people with different diseases. It is a type of selection bias termed after Joseph Berkeson who described it.

questions.stem: An epidemiologist plans to conduct a prospective study instead of a retrospective study. Which of the following disadvantages does he aim to eliminate by conducting this study?
questions.explanation:
Recall bias can be eliminated in a prospective study.
Recall bias is also called memory bias. It is widely seen in retrospective (case-control) studies as extensive history is taken from the participants.

questions.stem: A study conducted in a group revealed that consumption of alcohol increases the risk of esophageal cancer, but it may be actually due to cigarette smoking. This happens due to:
questions.explanation:
In this scenario, cigarette smoking is related to both the outcome of esophageal cancer and consumption of alcohol. Thus, this is an example of a confounding factor.
A confounding factor is defined as one which is associated with both exposure and outcome and is distributed unequally in study and control groups. In this study to determine the role of alcohol in the etiology of esophageal cancer, smoking is considered as a confounding factor because:
It is associated with the consumption of alcohol (exposure).
It is an independent risk factor for oesophageal cancer (outcome).
In these conditions, the effects of alcohol consumption can be determined only if the influence of smoking is neutralized by matching.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false regarding confounding factor?
options: It can be reduced by matching
It is associated individually with both cause and effect
It is distributed equally in both study and control groups
It is associated with the exposure of the study
questions.explanation:
A confounding factor is a factor that is associated with both exposure and diseases and is distributed unequally in study and control groups. It can be reduced by matching.
For example, if the study is that a sedentary lifestyle can lead to coronary artery diseases, then age can act as a confounding factor as it is individually linked to both sedentary lifestyle and coronary artery diseases.

questions.stem: A researcher is planning to conduct a study to investigate the relationship between oral contraceptives and breast cancer. He wants to remove age as a confounding factor. Which of the following methods will not help him reduce this bias?
questions.explanation:
Deletion is not a method to reduce confounding. Methods to reduce confounding are:
At the time of designing the study:
Randomization
Matching
Restriction
At the time of analysis:
Stratification
Statistical modelings like regression analysis, multivariate analysis, and the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel method.

questions.stem: Matching is done for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Matching helps only in removing the known confounding factors.
Matching is the process by which controls are selected in a way that they are similar to cases in certain pertinent variables (e.g., age) that are known to influence the outcome of the disease. If not adequately matched for comparability, these variables could confound the results.

questions.stem: Which among the following is not a type of matching?
questions.explanation:
There is no type of matching called collective matching. Types of matching:
Group matching: It is also called frequency matching. It is done when a large stratum is used for study and a 1:1 ratio of cases and controls can be achieved.
Individual matching: It is also called matching by pairs. It can be done when the study is small and more controls can be selected for one case.

questions.stem: An epidemiologist determines to evaluate the strength of association between asbestos exposure and mesothelioma in a case-control study. Which of the following variables would he use for it?
questions.explanation:
Odds ratio (OR), also known as cross-product ratio, is used to measure the strength of association between risk factor (asbestos exposure) and outcome (mesothelioma) in case-control studies.
A case-control study yields only odds ratio and not incidence or relative risk.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about the odds ratio?
options: It is obtained from case-control studies
It is a measure of strength of association
questions.explanation: An odds ratio (OR) of 1 indicates that there is no association or that the event is likely in both the groups.

questions.stem: A case-control study was done among 500 lung cancer patients and 400 controls. The study groups had 400 and 50 smokers respectively. Calculate the odds ratio.
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the odds ratio (OR) is 28. The given data is represented as:
Odds Ratio = ad/bc
= (400 x 350) / (50 x 100)
= (4 x 35)/5
= 4 x 7
= 28

questions.stem: A research scholar is preparing to do a prospective cohort study in a hospital to evaluate the association of H. pylori with inflammatory bowel disease. Which of the following measures must she take, before starting the study?
options: Enrol all patients taking proton pump inhibitors
Enrol all patients on whom endoscopy was done
Exclude all patients diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease
Exclude all patients with positive urea breath test for H. pylori
questions.explanation: All patients diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) must be excluded from a prospective cohort study, as the study progresses from cause to effect. The study begins before the disease under study has occurred.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about cohort study?
options: It is always a prospective study design
Outcome is not present at the start of study
questions.explanation:
Although cohort studies are called prospective studies, there are subtypes of cohort studies that do not follow the prospective study design like historical (retrospective) cohort studies.
Framingham Heart Study is one of the most famous long-term cardiovascular prospective cohort studies.

questions.stem: Hawthorne effect is seen in which of the following studies?
questions.explanation: Hawthorne effect is seen in cohort studies. It refers to the phenomenon when study subjects change or alter their behaviour during the course of the study, which results in different outcomes and underestimation of risks.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of the incidence of the disease in the exposed to that of the non-exposed?
questions.explanation: The ratio of incidence of disease or death among exposed to that among the non-exposed is called relative risk (RR).

questions.stem: Calculate the risk ratio when the incidence of the disease in exposed is 30 and that in non-exposed is 5.
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, risk ratio or relative risk (RR) is 6.
Here, the incidence of disease in the exposed is 30 and that in the non-exposed is 5. Thus, RR = 30/5 = 6.

questions.stem: A cohort study was conducted among 10,000 smokers and 10,000 non-smokers. They were followed up over a period of 20 years. It was found that 100 of the smokers and 10 of the non-smokers developed oral squamous cell carcinoma. Calculate the relative risk.
questions.explanation:
The relative risk in the given scenario is 10.
Here, the incidence in exposed is 0.01 (100/10000). Incidence in non-exposed is 0.001
(10/10000).
Relative Risk = Incidence in exposed/ Incidence in non-exposed = 0.01/0.001 = 10.

questions.stem: While testing the deleterious health hazards on a group of people after giving a new drug and a placebo, the following results were obtained as tabulated. Based on these results, which of the following is true?
options: Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.1
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 10% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.˜
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 10
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 10% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is ˜

In the given scenario, absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.1.

Relative risk reduction (RRR) = 1 – Relative risk. In this scenario, RRR = 1 – 0.˜ = 0.1 or 10%. Incidence of a disease is the absolute risk of contracting it.

questions.stem: The difference between the incidence of disease among exposed and incidence among non exposed is given by which of the following variables?
questions.explanation:
The difference between the incidence of disease among exposed and incidence among non-exposed is given by attributable risk.
Attributable risk is often expressed as a percentage.

questions.stem: A study conducted among smokers shows that 80% of the cases of lung cancer are due to cigarette smoking. Which of the following variables indicates this?
questions.explanation: Attributable risk indicates to what extent the disease under study can be attributed to the exposure. Here, cigarette smoking is attributed to be the cause of 80% of lung cancers in smokers.

questions.stem: A study found that the incidence of bladder carcinoma is 5 times higher in smokers than in non smokers. Calculate the attributable risk.
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the attributable risk (AR) is 80%.
Taking the incidence of disease in non-exposed as x, the incidence of disease in exposed would be 5x.
Attributable risk (AR) would be given as [(5x - x)/5x] x 100 = 80%.

questions.stem: In a population of ˜000 people, 2100 are alcoholics. 70 alcoholics and 23 non-alcoholics developed cirrhosis. What is the attributable risk?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the attributable risk (AR) is ˜0%. Number of people exposed (to alcohol) = 2100
Number of people not exposed (to alcohol) = 6˜00 Incidence of cirrhosis among exposed = 70/2100 (IExposed)
Incidence of cirrhosis among non-exposed = 23/6˜00 (INon-exposed)
Attributable risk (AR) = [ ( IExposed - INon-exposed) / IExposed ]*100
= [ (70/2100 - 23/6˜00) / (70/2100)] *100
= [ ˜ / 10 ] *100
= ˜0
Thus, the attributable risk (AR) is ˜0%.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the numerator in the formula for population-attributable risk?
options: Incidence among exposed minus incidence among non-exposed
Incidence among non-exposed minus incidence among exposed
Incidence in the total population minus incidence among non-exposed
Incidence in the total population minus incidence among exposed
questions.explanation:
Incidence in the total population minus incidence among non-exposed is the numerator in population-attributable risk (PAR).
[[IMG:1]]
Population attributable risk is obtained from cohort studies. It provides an estimate of the amount by which the disease could be reduced in that population if the suspected factor was eliminated or modified.

questions.stem: A study was done in the Indian population to correlate the deaths due to myocardial infarction and dietary practices. What is this type of study known as?
questions.explanation:
This is an example of an ecological study. As the study was done in the Indian population, it can be inferred that population was taken as the unit of the study.
The study was done to correlate the deaths and dietary practices, and hence ecological studies are also called correlational studies.

questions.stem: Which among the following is the weakest study design to prove causation?
questions.explanation:
Ecological studies take a population as a unit. They provide the weakest evidence for causality because of extrapolation to individuals from regional data.
Randomized control trials (RCTs) provide the strongest design amongst the options given. Case-control and cohort studies have moderate ability to provide evidence for causality.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: What kind of bias is implied by assigning group characteristics to people which they may not possess as individuals?
questions.explanation: An ecological fallacy results when characteristics of the group are assigned inappropriately to individuals.

In a clinical trial to evaluate a drug, randomisation was done before starting the trial. What is the purpose behind this?
options: The two groups will be similar in prognostic factors
The clinician has no control over the allocation of participants in each group
The clinician can predict in advance which treatment the subjects will receive
The sample may be referenced to a known population

options: Baseline characteristics are similar in both arms
Investigator’s bias is minimized by double blinding
The sample size required depends upon the hypothesis
The dropouts from the trial are not included in the analysis

questions.stem: A researcher decided to use double-blinding in his trial evaluating two new therapies for cystic fibrosis. What is the characteristic feature of this concept?
options: Study and control groups are blinded
Observer and group being observed are blinded
Group members and analyzer are blinded

A new drug for multiple sclerosis is undergoing clinical trials where its therapeutic efficacy is being confirmed and adverse reactions are being monitored. Which of the following phases is the drug most likely in?
In which of the following phases is the maximum drug failure rate seen?
The maximum tolerable dose of a new drug for Alzheimer's disease is to be evaluated. In which of the following phases is this done?

A hypothesis stating that people who continue to smoke are at a higher risk of developing lung carcinoma than those who have quit is to be tested. Which of the following study designs would you choose for this purpose?

What does evidence-based medicine refer to?
options: Use of experiments to prove the cause of a disease
Use of clinical trials to prove safety of drugs
Use of research findings for taking decisions about patient care
Use of behavioral modification to prevent disease

Which of the following is incorrect about systematic reviews?

options: File drawer effect can be seen here
It increases the statistical power by increasing sample size
Apples and oranges effect can be seen here
Its validity does not depend on the quality of the systematic review

For what purpose were knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) studies first used in India?

chapters.title: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemiology

questions.stem: What is the host in which a parasite passes through its sexual stages of maturity called?
questions.explanation:
A host in which a parasite passes through its sexual stage of maturity is called the definitive host or primary host.
A host in which a parasite exists in the larval or asexual form is called an intermediate host or secondary host.
A host which acts as the only source of development for a parasite is called the obligate host.
Note: A host in which the organism remains alive but no development occurs is called a transport host.

questions.stem: For which of the following diseases is man the dead-end host?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, man is the dead-end host for tetanus and rabies.
A dead-end host is a host from which the infectious agent lacks a portal of exit to continue its propagation.
Humans are dead-end hosts for :
Rabies
Tetanus
Bubonic Plague
Trichinosis

questions.stem: While studying a disease, you find that it affects both humans and lower vertebrates and can be transmitted in either direction. How would you classify this disease?
questions.explanation:
A disease that affects both humans and lower vertebrates and which can be transmitted in either direction is classified as amphixenosis. E.g, Trypanosoma cruzi and Schistosoma japonicum.
It is a type of zoonoses. Zoonoses are diseases that are transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans.
Other types of zoonoses include:
Anthropozoonoses - infections that are transmitted to man from vertebrates. E.g., Rabies, plague etc.
Zooanthroponoses - infections that are transmitted to vertebrates from humans. E.g., Human tuberculosis in cattle.
Epizootic disease refers to an outbreak or epidemic of a disease in an animal population, often with the implication that it may also affect human populations. Enzootic disease is an endemic occurring in animals.
Note: Epornithic diseases are those diseases which are epidemic in bird populations. E.g., Psittacosis.

questions.stem: What is a disease imported to an area from another called?
questions.explanation:
Exotic diseases are those imported into a country where they do not occur usually. E.g, rabies in the United Kingdom.
Enzootic diseases are those which are endemic in animals. E.g, anthrax, brucellosis. Epornithic disease refers to an epidemic in birds. E.g, psittacosis.
Epizootic disease refers to an outbreak of a disease or an epidemic in animals with the implication that it may affect humans. E.g, Q fever, influenza.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a disease that has a haphazard occurrence?
questions.explanation:
Sporadic diseases occur in a haphazard and irregular manner from time to time.
Endemic refers to the constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.
Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.
Pandemic is an epidemic occurring over a wide area, crossing international boundaries, and usually affecting a large number of people.
Note: Opportunistic infections are those that occur in the presence of immune suppression or deficiency like cytomegalovirus.

questions.stem: In a community, there are usually 40-50 reported cases of dengue every week. This week, there were 48 reported cases. This would classify as:
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is an example of an endemic disease.
Endemic diseases are those that have a constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.
Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.
Outbreak carries the same definition of an epidemic, but is often used for a more limited geographic area.
Sporadic diseases occur in a haphazard and irregular manner from time to time.

questions.stem: The following are the disease frequencies in a population. Based on the number of cases which of the following is the correct match?
questions.explanation:
Disease 1- the cases have been almost the same so it has to be endemic.
Disease 2- there is an alarming increase in the number of cases. It has to be an epidemic. Disease 3- the number of cases has decreased without any explanation so it has to be sporadic. Epidemic refers to the occurrence of a disease in excess of expected frequency.
A pandemic is an epidemic affecting a large population over a large geographical area crossing international boundaries.
An endemic disease is a regularly occurring disease in a population in expected frequency without any importation from outside.
Sporadic diseases present as scattered cases of infection without relation temporally/spatially.

questions.stem: Surveillance data of an endemic disease reveals that most of the children in the area had been affected and had to be hospitalised. However, most of the adults remained asymptomatic carriers. Which category does this disease belong to?
questions.explanation:
The disease in question belongs to the category of holoendemic diseases. In such diseases, a higher prevalence and pathogenic response are seen among the children in an area. The adults tend to be either asymptomatic carriers or show reduced damage by the disease process. E.g, malaria.
An endemic disease is a disease that is present constantly in a population or in a given area without importation from outside. E.g, kala-azar in Bihar.
A hyperendemic disease is a disease that is constantly present at high incidence and prevalence among all groups in a population. E.g, dengue in India.
A syndemic is the aggregation of two or more concurrent or sequential epidemics or disease clusters in a population with biological interactions, which exacerbate the prognosis and burden of disease. It is also known as a synergistic epidemic.
Note: Quasiendemic is not a term used in infectious disease epidemiology.

questions.stem: In which of the following diseases is subclinical infection not seen?
questions.explanation:
Subclinical infection is not seen in measles. It always causes the development of overt signs and symptoms.
Subclinical infection refers to an inapparent, covert, missed or abortive case. The host harbours and sheds the infectious agent but does not develop signs and symptoms of the disease.
Subclinical infections are seen in diseases like:
Hepatitis A
Diphtheria
Japanese encephalitis
Rubella
Subclinical infections can only be detected by laboratory tests. They frequently occur during a person’s lifetime and are responsible for the immunity shown by humans to a variety of disease-producing microbes.
Note: Subclinical cases should be differentiated from latent infections. In a latent infection, the host does not shed the organism but it lies dormant without signs and symptoms.

questions.stem: In which of the following states will the host not shed the infectious organism?
questions.explanation:
The host does not shed the infectious organism in case of a latent infection. This is defined as a state in which the host does not show signs and symptoms of the disease and does not shed the organism.
It can be seen in conditions like herpes simplex, ancylostomiasis, infections due to slow viruses, Brill-Zinsser disease, etc.
Subclinical infection is a state where the host harbours the infectious agent without developing signs and symptoms but sheds the infectious agent. This state is seen in conditions like hepatitis A, rubella, mumps, etc.
Healthy carriers are those who had subclinical infections and later developed a carrier state without suffering from the overt disease. This state is seen in: (mnemonic: CM - DPT)
Cholera
Meningitis
Diphtheria
Polio
Typhoid
Convalescent carriers are those which shed the infectious agent during the convalescent phase/recovery phase. Such carriers are seen in diphtheria, typhoid, cholera, pertussis, etc.

questions.stem: While in a health camp, you notice a child with fever and rash. On subsequent history, you find out that similar symptoms occurred in her friend 6 days back. How will you epidemiologically categorise the child you examined?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the child is categorised as the index case. It is the first case that comes to the notice of an investigator or physician.
The primary case is the first case of a communicable disease introduced into a population unit. A secondary case is one that develops after contact with the primary case.
A suspect case refers to a patient who has all the features of the disease but has not been diagnosed with it yet.
Note: There is no such term as tertiary case.

questions.stem: You are part of a research programme for COVID-19 and are asked to define the median incubation period. How will you define it?
options: Interval between onset of symptoms in primary and secondary cases
Time required for 50% of cases to occur following exposure
Interval between exposure and the occurrence of the first symptom
Time required for the start of pathogenesis following exposure
questions.explanation:
The median incubation period is the time required for 50% of the cases to occur following exposure. The median incubation period of COVID-19 of approximately 5 days.
Incubation period is the time interval between invasion of the infectious agent and the appearance of the first symptom or sign in the body. It is termed as the latent period in non-infectious diseases.
Incubation period depends upon:
Generation time of pathogen
Portal of entry
Infective dose
Individual susceptibility Incubation period is useful for :
Tracing the source of infection and contacts.
Determining the period of surveillance or quarantine.
Planning immunization.
Identification of point source or propagated epidemics.
Determining the prognosis.

questions.stem: In a school of 100 children, a child developed measles. Four days later, 3 of her classmates developed measles. What do these intervening four days correspond to?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the first child is the primary case and her classmates are the secondary cases. Hence, the interval between them developing the disease i.e., the intervening four days, is called the serial interval.
The time interval between the onset of the primary case and the secondary case is called serial interval.
By collecting information about a whole series of such disease onsets, the distribution of the secondary cases can be made. From this information, an approximation of the incubation period can be done.
Lead time/lead interval refers to the period between the first possible time of detection and the usual time of diagnosis.
Incubatory interval/ incubation period refers to the time period between invasion of a pathogen to appearance of the first sign or symptom.
Latent interval/ latent period refers to the period between disease initiation to detection of the disease. It is usually used for non-infectious diseases and is equivalent to the incubation period.
Note :
Primary case is the first case of a communicable disease introduced into a population unit.
Secondary case is one that develops after contact with the primary case.
Index case is the first case that comes to the notice of an investigator or physician.

questions.stem: The time interval between which of the following is called generation time?
options: Development of primary case and secondary case
Receipt of infection by host and maximum infectivity of the same host
Infection and first sign or symptom
Infection and initiation of pathogenesis inside the host
questions.explanation: Generation time is the time interval between receipt of infectious agent by the host and the point of maximum infectivity of the same host.

questions.stem: For which of the following diseases is soil not a reservoir?
questions.explanation:
The main reservoir of the coccobacilli belonging to the genus Brucella that cause brucellosis are animals like sheep, cattle, horses, goats, whales, and dogs.
A reservoir is the environment (e.g. soil, humans, animals, water, etc.) where the infectious agent grows and multiplies (natural habitat) and from where it can be transmitted to a susceptible host.
A source is an animal, object, human or substance which acts as an immediate mode of transmission and may or may not be a part of the reservoir.
Option A: Coccidiomycosis is also called Valley fever and the causative fungi belong to the Coccidiodes. The main reservoir of this organism is soil.
Option B: Bacillus anthracis is a soil commensal and is also found on the hides and dried skins of infected animals.
Option C: The natural reservoir for the fungi causing mycetoma is soil.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not communicable during the later part of the period marked 3 in the below image? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The period marked 3 in the figure is the incubation period while the later part of the period represents subclinical infection. Rabies is not communicable during its incubation period as it is transmitted from the saliva of a rabid animal through bite or scratch.
An incubatory carrier state is one in which carriers shed the organism during the incubation period of the disease, especially during the later parts of it.
Examples of diseases showing incubatory carrier state are:
Measles
Polio
Mumps
Whooping cough
Diphtheria
Influenza
Hepatitis A
Carriers of a disease are classified by the following:
Type: Incubatory, convalescent or healthy.
Duration: Temporary or chronic.
Portal of exit: Urinary, respiratory, intestinal or others.
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: Which of the following carriers shed the organism for indefinite periods?
questions.explanation:
Chronic carriers are those who shed or excrete the organism for indefinite periods. Carriers are classified into chronic carriers and temporary carriers based on the duration.
Organisms may be shed continuously or intermittently in chronic carriers. The duration of the carrier state also depends on the disease. Chronic carrier state is seen in typhoid, hepatitis B, gonorrhea, malaria, etc.
Temporary carriers are classified into:
Incubatory carriers - Those that shed the organism during the incubation period of the disease, especially during the later parts of it. It is seen in measles, mumps, polio, etc.
Healthy carriers - Those who suffer from subclinical infections and develop a carrier state without developing the overt disease. It is seen in polio, meningococcal meningitis, cholera, diphtheria, etc.
Convalescent carriers - Those that shed the organism during recovery or convalescence. It is seen in typhoid.
Paradoxical carrier refers to a carrier who acquires the pathogen from another carrier. Note: Pseudo-carriers are carriers of avirulent organisms.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases does not show vertical transmission?
questions.explanation:
Tetanus does not show vertical or transplacental transmission.
Transmission of diseases or non-infectious agents transplacentally is called vertical transmission. Diseases that show this type of transmission include:
Herpes
HIV
Rubella
Varicella
Apart from diseases, non-infectious agents like lithium, thalidomide, stilbestrol, etc. can cross the placenta and lead to the development of congenital anomalies in a foetus.
Note: Neonatal tetanus occurs as a result of the failure to use aseptic techniques in managing the umbilical stump, unclean hands, and instruments or contamination by dirt, straw, or other nonsterile materials in the delivery field. Immunisation of pregnant women can prevent this disease via the transplacental transport of immunoglobulins.

questions.stem: Which among the following is false about droplet transmission?
options: All droplets can travel only as far as 3 feet
Droplets are usually larger than 5 microns
It is a type of direct transmission
Basic ventilation decreases the potential for this type of transmission
questions.explanation:
Droplet nuclei can travel as far as 6 feet, whereas a droplet (particle > 5m) travels
<30-60cm, as recent studies have shown.
Droplets are a mode of direct transmission of infectious agents. They are formed from saliva and nasopharyngeal secretions released during coughing, sneezing, or speaking into the surrounding atmosphere. The expelled droplets may impinge directly upon the conjunctiva, oro-respiratory mucosa or skin of close contact. This mode of transmission is seen in common cold, diphtheria, etc.
Proper basic ventilation and prevention of overcrowding reduce the potential for this type of transmission.

questions.stem: What is the maximum size of airborne droplet nuclei?
questions.explanation:
Droplet nuclei are sized less than or equal to 5 microns.
They may be formed by evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or be generated purposefully by a variety of atomizing devices (aerosols). They are capable of indirect airborne transmission of diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, etc.
The droplet nuclei may remain airborne for long periods of time, some retaining and others losing infectivity or virulence. These small particles when inhaled are capable of reaching the alveoli and getting retained there.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a method of direct transmission of communicable diseases?
questions.explanation:
Airborne transmission by droplet nuclei is not a method of direct transmission of diseases. It is a method of indirect transmission of diseases.
Droplet nuclei are tiny particles of size 1-5 microns range that may be formed by either due to evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or are formed from aerosols.
These droplet nuclei remain airborne for long periods of time and can transmit diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, Q fever and other respiratory infections.
Droplet transmission, vertical transmission, and contact with soil are methods of direct transmission of diseases.
Differences between droplet and droplet nuclei are summarised below:
DROPLET NUCLEI | DROPLET
Indirect transmission | Direct transmission
It is the residue from evapora ted droplets | It is produced while coughing, sneezing, talking
<5microns in diameter | 5 microns in diameter
No need for close contact for transmission | Requires closeness and direct contact for transmission
Diseases transmitted: chicke npox, measles etc. | Diseases transmitted: diphth eria, meningococcal meningit is etc.

questions.stem: Spread of disease via which of the following is an example of an indirect mode of transmission?
questions.explanation:
The spread of a disease through contaminated food is an example of vehicle-borne transmission. It is an indirect mode of transmission.
Vehicle-borne transmission is the transmission of infectious agents through food, water and biological products (blood, plasma etc.). Of these, food and water are more frequent vehicles of transmission because they are used by everyone.
Mother to child transmission, droplet infection and transmission via dog bite are examples of direct modes of transmission.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about fomite-borne transmission is false?
options: It is an indirect mode of transmission
Transmission via contaminated food is an example of this
Hepatitis A is transmitted in this way
Routine disinfection can prevent such transmission
questions.explanation:
Fomites are objects other than water or food that can be contaminated by infectious agents and help in transmitting the disease. They include clothes, towels, linen, cups, plates, spoons, etc.
Fomites are an example of an indirect mode of transmission.
Some diseases transmitted by fomites include diphtheria, typhoid, hepatitis A, etc. Good public and personal hygiene can prevent this type of transmission.

questions.stem: What is the lodgement and development of an arthropod on the body surface called?
questions.explanation:
The lodgement and development of an arthropod on the body surface is called infestation. Infection is the entry and development or multiplication of an infectious agent in a host’s body.
Contamination is the presence of a disease agent on a body surface like clothes, toys, etc. and also in substances like food or water.
Colonization is the presence of a disease agent in or on a host, with growth and multiplication but without any overt clinical expression or detected immune response in the host at the time it is isolated.

questions.stem: An entomologist was studying a vector and the pathogen it transmits. He found that the pathogen underwent changes in number and morphology in the vector. What is this type of biological transmission called?
questions.explanation:
This type of biological transmission where a pathogen undergoes a change in number and morphology in a vector is called cyclo-propagative transmission.
Malaria is a disease whose causative organism (Plasmodium sp.) undergoes cyclo-propagative transmission. In malaria, the parasite undergoes both developmental changes and multiplication in the Anopheles mosquito (vector).

questions.stem: A patient with chronic lymphedema was found to have a positive DEC provocation test. Which type of biological transmission does the pathogen implicated here undergo?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the patient most likely has lymphatic filariasis. The causative organism of this disease (Wuchereria bancrofti) undergoes cyclo-developmental transmission.
Cyclo-developmental transmission is a transmission where the agent undergoes only developmental changes and not multiplication within the vector.
DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

questions.stem: You are a rural medical health officer investigating an epidemic. What is the correct sequence of steps you must follow?
questions.explanation:
Steps for the investigation of an epidemic are:
Verification of diagnosis
Confirmation of the existence of an epidemic
Defining the population at risk -
Obtaining a map of the area
Counting the population
Rapid search for all the cases -
Medical survey
Epidemiological case sheets
Searching for more cases
Data analysis on the basis of time, place and person
Formulation of hypothesis
Testing of hypothesis
Evaluation of ecological factors
Further investigation of the population at risk
Writing the report

questions.stem: You have been asked to write the final report following the investigation of a cholera epidemic. Which of the following will you not include in this report?
options: Usual number of cases that existed before the epidemic
questions.explanation:
The final report of an epidemic does not include the incubation period of the disease. The final report following the investigation of an epidemic should include:
Background information - Geography, climate, demography, socio-economic groups, health service organization, surveillance data and normal disease prevalence.
Historical data - Previous occurrences of the epidemic, the occurrence of any related diseases and discovery of the primary case in the present outbreak.
Methodology of investigations - Case definition, epidemiological questionnaires, collection and laboratory techniques.
Analysis of data - Clinical and epidemiological data, modes of transmission, laboratory data and all their interpretations.
Control measures - Strategy definitions, methodology of implementation, evaluation methods and preventive measures.

questions.stem: You have been sent to an area to study the ongoing typhoid epidemic. When will you declare the area to be free of the epidemic?
questions.explanation:
The area will be declared free of the typhoid epidemic when no new cases are reported for 28 days.
An area is declared free of an epidemic when there are no cases reported for twice the incubation period of the disease since the last case.
The incubation period of typhoid is 14 days. So, in the given scenario, the area will be declared free of the epidemic when no new cases are reported for twice the incubation period i.e., 14 x 2 = 28 days.

questions.stem: The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is known as the .
questions.explanation:
The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is called secondary attack rate.
It is calculated by the following formula:
Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)
Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and denominator. Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.

questions.stem: Following an outbreak of a disease, you are asked to calculate the secondary attack rate (SAR). What is the denominator you would use?
options: All people having history of contact with a case
All people susceptible in the entire area
All the people in contact with the primary case
All the close or exposed contacts those are susceptible
questions.explanation:
The denominator used for calculating SAR is all the close or exposed contacts that are susceptible.
The secondary attack rate is defined as the probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period.
It is calculated by the formula:
Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)
Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and denominator. Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.

questions.stem: A village has 100 children under the age of 5. The coverage of measles vaccination is 60%. Following a case of measles, 26 children developed measles. What is the secondary attack rate?
questions.explanation:
The secondary attack rate for the given scenario is 66%. The secondary attack rate (SAR) is given by:
(Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)
Here, number who developed the disease after exposure= 26 Susceptible population= 100 - 60 (vaccinated) - 1 (primary case) = 39
Therefore, SAR = 26 /39 x 100 = 66%. SAR is a measure of communicability.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is found to be positive for SARS-CoV-2. On contact tracing, 30 people have been identified as close contacts but none of them shows any symptoms or signs. What is the time duration for which they must be quarantined?
questions.explanation:
Quarantine is the limitation in freedom of movement of healthy contacts of cases, who have been exposed for a period that lasts as long as the maximal incubation period of the disease.
It is a primary level of prevention and falls under specific protection measures. The various types of quarantine are:
Absolute - Complete limitation of movement
Modified - Selective partial limitation of movement
Segregation - Observation of a group of persons in a population after separation

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of diseases and their periods of isolation is wrongly matched?
options: Rubella – 3 days after onset of rash
Chickenpox – 6 days after onset of rash
Herpes zoster – 6 days after onset of rash
Measles – Up to 5 days after onset of rash
questions.explanation:
Patients with rubella should be isolated for 7 days after they develop the rash.
Isolation is defined as separation, for the period of communicability of infected persons from others to prevent or limit transmission of the infectious agent.
In settings where women who are in their 1st trimester or sexually active or non-immune without contraception usage may be exposed, outbreak control measures should begin as soon as rubella is suspected and should not be postponed until laboratory confirmation of cases.
Note: Multiple sources have confimed the period of infectivity of measles which is from 4 days before the onset of rash to 5 days after the onset of rash.

questions.stem: A paradoxical carrier is defined as:
options: A person who sheds pathogens during incubation period
A carrier who acquired pathogen from another carrier
A person who acquired pathogen from patient
A patient who became a carrier
questions.explanation:
A paradoxical carrier is a carrier that acquired a pathogen from another carrier.
Incubatory carriers are those who shed the infectious agents during the incubation period of the disease.
Convalescent carriers are those who continue to shed the disease agent during the period of convalescence.
Healthy carriers are those who had a subclinical infection and developed a carrier state without suffering from overt disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about herd immunity?
options: It refers to group protection beyond what is afforded by the protection of immunized individuals
Vaccination allows the possibility of 100% herd immunity against a disease
It is affected by presence and distribution of alternative animal hosts
It doesn’t protect the individual in the case of tetanus
questions.explanation:
It is not possible to achieve 100% herd immunity against a certain disease but studies have shown this is not necessary for disease control.
Herd structure is never constant. It is subject to constant variation because of new births, deaths and population mobility. An ongoing immunization programme will keep up the herd immunity at a very high level.

questions.stem: Herd immunity threshold does not vary with which of the following?
options: Efficacy of the vaccine for the disease
Number of vaccines for the disease
questions.explanation: Herd immunity threshold does not vary with the number of vaccines for the disease. It varies only due to the virulence of the disease, efficacy of the vaccine and contact parameter for the population.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about normal human immunoglobulin (NHIG)?
options: All live vaccines can be given simultaneously with NHIG.
They are used against measles and hepatitis A.
There should be a low IgA concentration in NHIG preparations.
Each NHIG fraction is obtained from at least 1,000 donors.
questions.explanation:
Live vaccines should generally be avoided for 12 weeks following an injection of normal human immunoglobulin (Ig). If a live vaccine has already been administered, the injection of normal human Ig should be delayed for 2 weeks.
NHIG is an antibody-rich fraction that is usually obtained from a pool of at least 1,000 donors. AN NHIG preparation must contain at least 90% intact IgG and minimal IgG aggregates with low IgA concentration. NHIG is commonly used to prevent measles and hepatitis A infections.
Specific human immunoglobulins are made from the plasma of patients who have recently recovered from an infection or are obtained from individuals who have been immunized against a specific infection. These preparations have a high antibody content against an individual infection and provide immediate protection.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about specific human immunoglobulins?
questions.explanation:
Specific human immunoglobulins or hyperimmune human Igs are obtained from selected donors that have high titres of the antibodies to the disease like those who have recovered from the disease.
It is commonly used in prophylaxis of chickenpox in highly susceptible individuals and in post-exposure prophylaxis of hepatitis B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about secondary booster immune response in comparison with primary response?
options: Antibody elicited tends to have a greater avidity to bind to the antigen
Antibody response is at a higher level
Antibody response is maintained for a longer period of time
questions.explanation:
Production of antibodies is faster in secondary booster response.
Primary response is the immune response developed when an antigen is administered for the first time to a person who has never been exposed to it. There is a latent period of 3-10 days before antibodies appear in the blood.
Secondary booster response is the immune response elicited by a booster dose. In comparison to a primary immune response, it has a shorter latent period, faster production of antibodies, and
an abundance of antibodies. The antibody response is maintained at higher levels for a longer period of time, and the antibody elicited tends to have a greater avidity or capacity to bind to the antigen.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about live vaccines?
options: Simultaneous administration of two live vaccines should be done in the same syringe
Two live vaccines can be administered simultaneously
Immuno-compromised state poses a contraindication to live vaccines
Live vaccines contain both major and minor antigens
questions.explanation:
Simultaneous administration of vaccines is defined as administering more than one vaccine on the same clinic day, at different anatomic sites. They are not combined in the same syringe.
Simultaneous administration of the most widely used live and inactivated vaccines does not result in decreased antibody responses or increased rates of adverse reaction. However, in children with functional or anatomic asplenia pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) and Menactra brand meningococcal conjugate vaccines should not be administered at the same visit; separate these vaccines by at least 4 weeks.
Advantages of simultaneous administration of vaccines:
The organisms multiply in the host and thus, the antigenic dose is larger than what is injected.
They have all the major and minor antigenic components.
Live vaccines should not be administered to those with an immunocompromised state, since they may cause severe systemic disease by way of viremia/bacteriemia.
Note: If live vaccines are not given simultaneously, they must be spaced as follows-
The administration of two live parenteral vaccines or live intranasal influenza vaccines must be separated by at least 4 weeks (28 days).
If two live vaccines are given less than 4 weeks apart, the second vaccine should be repeated in four weeks. This is because the live vaccine given first can interfere with the second vaccine, and the person may not develop active immunity to the second vaccine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a killed vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Yellow fever vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine.
Injectable polio vaccine (Salk vaccine), pertussis vaccine, and rabies vaccine are killed vaccines.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to administration of inactivated or killed vaccines?
questions.explanation:
The only absolute contraindication to administration of an inactivated or killed vaccine is severe local or general reaction to a previous dose of the vaccine.
Inactivated or killed vaccines are made from growing cultures of the organism and then inactivating them with heat or chemicals.They activate the channels of active immunity after injection and are less efficacious than live vaccines. Multiple doses or booster doses are usually required to produce an adequate antibody response.
Killed vaccines can be given to immune-compromised individuals and in pregnancy as the infective agent is inactivated and cannot grow.
Egg allergy is not an absolute contraindication to the administration of an inactivated or killed vaccine.

questions.stem: Which of the following are live vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Yellow fever vaccine and Sabin vaccine (oral polio vaccine) are live vaccines.
HBV and HPV vaccines are recombinant vaccines. Tetanus vaccine is a toxoid vaccine.

questions.stem: What should be the minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines?
questions.explanation:
The minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines is 4 weeks.
This is because decreasing the interval between two doses may interfere with the antibody response and protection. Thus, live vaccines can either be given on the same day according to the schedule or 4 weeks apart.
Note: In Park 27th ed. the minimum interval between two live vaccines is given as 3 weeks. However, several other standard sources including CDC and UNDP suggested an interval of 4 weeks. When both are given in options, it is recommended to mark 4 weeks as the correct answer.

questions.stem: In which of the following diseases should active and passive immunisation not be done together?
questions.explanation:
Active and passive immunization should not be done together for measles as the vaccine used is a live vaccine.
Live vaccines should generally be avoided for 12 weeks following an injection of normal human immunoglobulin (Ig). If a live vaccine has already been administered, the injection of normal human Ig should be delayed for 2 weeks.
Note: In the case of measles alone, the recommended interval between administration of Measles immunoglobulins and Live measles vaccine is about 6 months in a non-immunocompromised individual and 8 months in an immunocompromised individual.

questions.stem: What is the main drawback of polysaccharide-based vaccines?
options: They cause severe pain at the injection site
The immune responses elicited are serotype specific
It cannot be conjugated with proteins to enhance immunogenicity
The rate of adverse reactions is very high
questions.explanation:
Polysaccharide-based vaccines stimulate an antibody response against the surface polysaccharide of the pathogenic-capsulated bacteria. The polysaccharide structure varies not only between bacteria of different species but also between different strains within a single species. Thus, a limitation of these vaccines is that the immune responses are serotype-specific.
If these vaccines are conjugated with proteins, they are given the capability of eliciting a stronger immune response. Multivalent formulations of both polysaccharide-based vaccines and conjugated vaccines are required to achieve protection against multiple serotypes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a subunit vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis B vaccine is an example of a subunit vaccine made using HBsAg.
Subunit vaccines are produced from macromolecules derived from immunogenic components of organisms by recombinant DNA technology. E.g., HPV vaccine (uses L1 major capsid protein) and hepatitis B vaccine (uses HBsAg).
BCG is a live attenuated vaccine, IPV is an inactivated vaccine and DPT has diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and a killed pertussis component.

questions.stem: You are a medical officer conducting an ANC camp in a rural village near Hubli, Karnataka. Which of the following vaccines would you not administer to a pregnant woman?
questions.explanation:
Yellow fever vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy in non-endemic areas. It is a live vaccine and most live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy unless the risk of infection is much greater than the risk of harm to the fetus.
Note: Yellow fever vaccine is not an absolute contraindication as it is administered in certain endemic areas and in outbreaks

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed to have an allergy to eggs. Administration of which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in this patient?
questions.explanation: Influenza and yellow fever vaccines are contraindicated in patients having an allergy to eggs.

questions.stem: A newborn baby is HIV + and symptomatic. Which of the following vaccines must not be given to her?
questions.explanation:
BCG vaccine must not be administrated to HIV-infected infants who are symptomatic despite the presence of high TB prevalence. Since BCG is a live vaccine, it significantly increases the risk of disseminated TB in a symptomatic HIV+ infant.
However, asymptomatic infants who are HIV+ can be given BCG, provided the risk of contracting TB is high in that region. In areas of low TB prevalence or risk, the BCG vaccine is avoided.
[[IMG:1]]
WHO recommendations for administering live vaccines in symptomatic HIV+ patients:
Measles vaccine (or MMR) is allowed even in the symptomatic stage of HIV infection (except in the terminal phase), so as to prevent serious and life-threatening wild measles virus disease. Avoid MMR only if CD4+ < 15% (severely immunocompromised).
IPV is an inactivated vaccine and must be used as an alternative to OPV.

questions.stem: Which of the following side effects is most likely to develop in a newborn, following BCG vaccination?
questions.explanation:
Ulceration is the most common side effect post BCG vaccination.
Following vaccination, the local tissue response begins in 2-3 weeks and results in scar formation and healing within 3 months. Side effects most commonly seen include ulceration at the vaccination site and regional lymphadenitis. Some vaccine strains may also rarely cause osteomyelitis.
In immunocompromised states, disseminated BCG infection can occur.
The image below shows the typical adverse effcts seen following BCG vaccination:
Regional lymphadenopathy
Suppurative lymphadenopathy with fistula
Ulcer at injection site
Cold abscess at inject site
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: A child who had recently received the BCG vaccine comes to you with complaints of fever, pain and swelling at the injection site. You suspect a localised abscess formation. Which of the following steps should be avoided in the treatment of this child?
options: Incision and application of INH powder
Incision and application of PAS powder
questions.explanation:
There is no need for systemic treatment with INH in case of a local abscess formation after BCG vaccination.
If there is a local abscess formation following BCG vaccination, it should be treated by aspiration. If it does not clear, then it should be incised and INH or PAS powder should be applied daily to the site. The patient should be assured of the harmless nature of the lesion.

questions.stem: A complete blood count was obtained for a patient after they were administered vaccine X. The report is shown below. Which of the following options is most likely to be vaccine X?
questions.explanation: The lab report shows a low platelet count or thrombocytopenia. This is a possible adverse effect of the MMR vaccine.

questions.stem: Persistent inconsolable crying can be a result of administration of which of the following vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Persistent inconsolable crying is usually seen after DPT vaccine. It is mostly attributed to the pertussis fraction of the vaccine.
It usually lasts for 3 hours and settles after a day or so. Other adverse effects of the DTP vaccine include neurologic effects like encephalitis and encephalopathies.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about the DPT vaccine?
options: Adult preparation contains a lower dose of diphtheria than the pediatric version
Whole killed bacteria of Bordetella pertussis has an adjuvant effect
The whole-cell killed B. pertussis component is encephalogenic
Presence of H. influenzae type b component increases its immunogenicity
questions.explanation:
H. influenzae type b (Hib) is not a component of the DPT vaccine and hence cannot affect its immunogenicity. It is a component of the pentavalent vaccine.
The DPT vaccine is made up of diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus vaccines. The pertussis component in DPT vaccine enhances the potency of the diphtheria toxoid. Both whole-cell killed
B. pertussis and acellular pertussis component have this adjuvant effect. The only difference is that whole-cell killed B. pertussis is encephalitogenic and immunity is short-lasting, while the acellular pertussis component (DTaP) is devoid of neurological complications.
There are two types of DPT vaccines - plain and adsorbed. Adsorption is usually carried out on a mineral carrier like aluminium phosphate or hydroxide. Adsorbed vaccines are more immunogenic and recommended by WHO for national vaccination programmes.

questions.stem: A worried mother brings her baby to your PHC saying her child has gone limp. She mentions the child had recently been given some oral drops as part of a mass vaccination campaign. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the baby's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of paralysis and the likely cause is vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis following OPV administration.
This is a rare side effect of OPV. Acute-onset flaccid paralysis occurs within 4 to 30 days of receipt of the vaccine in these cases or within 4 to 75 days after contact with a vaccine recipient.

questions.stem: A patient presents with complaints of severe aching pain and weakness in his left arm and shoulder. He mentions he had recently been administered a vaccine in his left arm, but he does not remember the name of the vaccine. Which of the following could be the most common cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of brachial neuritis which is a known complication of the tetanus vaccine.
Brachial neuritis is a dysfunction of nerves supplying the arm and shoulder without the involvement of the rest of the nervous system. It presents with a deep, steady, severe aching pain in the shoulder and arm followed by weakness and wasting in arm and shoulder muscles. Sensory loss may also be present. It is treated symptomatically by analgesics.

questions.stem: Select the wrongly matched pair of excipients and vaccines.
questions.explanation:
Formaldehyde is not used in the BCG vaccine. It is used in IPV and diphtheria and tetanus vaccines.
Excipients (other vaccine constituents) include: Adjuvants: serve to enhance the immune reaction to the vaccine , Stabilizers : stabilize and prolong the shelf-life of the vaccine and
Preservatives : preserve the components. Some examples are listed below:
As stabilizing agents-
MgCl2 - OPV
MgSO4 - measles
Lactose-sorbitol and sorbitol-gelatine
To prevent microbial growth and contamination-
Thiomersal- DPT, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), rabies, influenza, and meningococcal diseases. It contains very small amounts of organic mercury.
Neomycin- MMR and IPV
Other preservatives-
2-phenoxyethanol - IPV
Phenol - Typhoid vaccine

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about adjuvants in vaccines?
options: Immune response is increased by degree or duration by their use
They are used in HPV vaccines
There is a high incidence of side effects with their use
They help in the reduction of amount of immunogens in vaccines
questions.explanation:
Side effects are rare with the use of adjuvants in vaccines.
Adjuvants are substances that are added to vaccines to enhance their immunogenicity by degree and/or duration. They help in the reduction of the amount of immunogen in vaccines or in the number of doses required to achieve immunity.
Aluminium salts are the most commonly used adjuvants. Adjuvants are used in many vaccines like:
Anthrax vaccine
Hep A vaccine
Hep B vaccine
çapanese encephalitis vaccine
DT and DTaP
HPV vaccine
Pneumococcal vaccine

questions.stem: Which adjuvant is used in the DPT vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Aluminium is the adjuvant used in DPT vaccines.
The table below lists adjuvants used in human vaccines:
Name | Class | Components | Vaccine
Alum | Mineral salts | Aluminium phosphate, alumi nium hydroxide | Diphtheria, tetanus, pneumo coccus, HAV, HBV, anthrax, tick-borne encephalitis, Men C, HPV
