questions.stem: A child has come to you for the administration of the IPV vaccine, as part of his routine immunisation schedule. Which of the following antibiotics may be found in this vaccine?
questions.explanation:
IPV may contain trace amounts of streptomycin, neomycin or polymyxin B. MMR contain small amount of neomycin.
Antibiotics are used during vaccine manufacture to prevent bacterial contamination of tissue culture cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the most and least heat-sensitive vaccines respectively?
options: Sabin vaccine and hep B vaccine
çapanese encaphalitis vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine
Salk vaccine and hep B vaccine
questions.explanation: Oral polio (Sabin) vaccine is the most heat-sensitive vaccine. Hepatitis B vaccines are the least heat-sensitive alongside meningococcal A vaccine, freeze-dried Hib vaccine and pneumococcal vaccines.

questions.stem: Which of the following vaccines should be protected from sub-zero temperatures?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis B vaccine is sensitive to freezing and should be protected from sub-zero temperatures. Vaccines to be protected from freezing are as follows:
Hepatitis B
Cholera
DTaP-hepB-Hib-IPV (hexavalent)
DTwP-hepB-Hib (pentavalent)
Liquid Hib
IPV
Influenza, pneumococcal vaccines
Tetanus, DT, Td
Rotavirus (freeze-dried, least sensitive), the liquid form is resistant to freezing
HPV

questions.stem: What vaccines are supplied in the type of bottle given below? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]] 163
questions.explanation: The image shows an amber-colored vial. Vaccines like BCG and measles vaccine are sensitive to light and thus are supplied in such vials.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-electrical cold-chain equipment?
questions.explanation:
Cold boxes, vaccine carriers, and ice packs are some of the non-electrical components of the cold-chain system.
Cold boxes are insulated containers used for transportation and temporary storage of vaccines and ice packs. Vaccine carriers are usually not used for the storage of vaccines but for their transportation. Ice packs generally have two holes in them for placing vaccines. They are filled with water.
The below image shows a cold box containing vaccines and ice packs.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: What is the temperature maintained in the freezer compartment of the solar refrigerator battery drive?
questions.explanation:
The freezer compartment of the solar refrigerator battery drive is maintained at – 7 °C, and it is used to store mainly ice packs.
The vaccine storage compartment of this solar cold chain equipment is maintained at 2 to 8
°C. The other solar cold-chain equipment commonly used is the solar refrigerators direct drive, which uses the sun’s energy to freeze phase-change materials like water and then uses this formed
ice bank to keep the refrigerator cold.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about the device shown in the image below? 164 [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
options: Smaller ones are given to PHCs and the larger ones to district vaccine stores
They have temperature zones for different vaccines
Kata thermometer is used to record temperature inside this device
These devices are provided with baskets to store vaccines
questions.explanation:
The image shown in the question is of an ice-lined refrigerator (ILR). Dial or digital thermometers are used to record temperatures inside an ice-lined refrigerator.
ILRs are the main method of vaccine storage in primary health centers. They are an important part of the cold chain and they maintain a temperature of 2 to 8 °C for the storage of vaccines.
They have different temperature zones for different vaccines. The upper zone is for
freeze-sensitive vaccines like cholera, hep B, rotavirus(liquid), etc while the lower zone is for heat-sensitive vaccines like OPV, measles, etc.
All vaccines are kept in the basket provided with ILR. Vaccines like OPV, BCG, measles, and çE can be kept at the bottom of the basket while, DPT, TT, Hep B, IPV, and pentavalent vaccines and diluents are kept in the upper part of the basket.

questions.stem: While working as a medical officer in a CHC, you experience a sudden power cut in your area due to which the ice-lined refrigerator loses power. What is the time taken for the temperature inside this equipment to rise to the maximum recommended temperature limit?
questions.explanation:
Hold-over time is the time taken by cold-chain equipment to raise the temperature inside it, during loss of power, to the maximum temperature limit in its recommended range. For an ice-lined refrigerator(ILR), this time depends on:
Ambient temperature
Frequency of opening the equipment
šuantity of vaccines kept inside with spacing
Condition of ice-pack lining The below image shows an ILR.
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
172

questions.stem: At what level is the risk of cold-chain failure the highest? 165
questions.explanation: The risk of cold chain failure is highest at the sub-centre and village levels. Thus, vaccines are not stored at the sub-centre and are supplied on the day of use.

questions.stem: Open vial policy is not applicable to which of the following vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Open vial policy is not applicable for BCG and measles vaccines. It is applicable for:
DPT
TT
Hepatitis B vaccine
OPV
Pentavalent vaccine
Rotavirus vaccine (New version with the VVM on the side)

questions.stem: What are the devices given below used to measure? [[IMG:1]]
options: Disintegration of vaccine constituents due to temperature
questions.explanation:
The image shown is of vaccine vial monitors (VVM), which measure the cumulative heat exposure of the vaccine.
VVMs are heat-sensitive indicators that are routinely used to monitor vaccine viability as the vaccine vial moves across the supply chain. They record cumulative heat exposure through
a gradual change in color. If the color of the inner square is the same or is darker than the outer circle, the vaccine has been exposed to too much heat and should be discarded.

questions.stem: You are preparing to administer the BCG vaccine to a newborn at a PHC. Before administering the vaccine, you check the vaccine vial monitor. In which of the following observations on the VVM, will you discard the vaccine? 166
options: Inner square has the same color as the outer circle
Inner circle has the same color as the outer square
Inner circle is lighter than the outer square
questions.explanation: A vaccine must be discarded if the VVM shows the inner square is the same color or darker than the outer circle.

questions.stem: Which of the following vaccine vials can be used based on the vaccine vial monitor (VVM) color changes shown? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
From the above image, only vials 1 and 2 can be used as the inner squares of the VVMs are lighter than the outer circles.
Vial 3 has crossed the discard point as the inner square and outer circle are the same color and thus cannot be used. Vial 4 cannot be used as the VVM shows a darker inner square compared to the outer circle.

questions.stem: You are volunteering in a vaccination camp. You perform a shake test before administering a particular vaccine. Which of the following is checked by this test?
questions.explanation:
The shake test is done to check for damage to vaccines that are sensitive to freezing temperatures. Steps to perform the shake test:
A frozen vaccine is used as a control vial and the vial suspected to be damaged by freezing is taken as the test vial.
Both are shaken after thawing and the rate of sedimentation is compared.
If the rate of sedimentation in the test vial is slower than that in the control vial, then it is usable and has not been damaged.
[[IMG:1]]
Some of the most widely used vaccines are freeze-sensitive. These include vaccines against:
Diphtheria
Tetanus
Pertussis
Haemophilus influenza type b (Liquid )
Hepatitis B

questions.stem: Which is the process designed to prevent microorganisms from reaching a protected environment?
questions.explanation:
Asepsis is the process designed to prevent microorganisms from reaching a protected environment.
Sterilization is a process of killing or removal of all living microorganisms either in the vegetative or spore state from an area or surface or a medium.
Decontamination is the process of rendering an article or area free of contaminants, including microbial, chemical, radioactive and other hazardous materials.
Disinfection is the process by which the destruction of microorganisms is achieved with the use of physical or chemical agents. Microbial forms like spores and some viruses may be resistant to certain disinfectants.

questions.stem: All of the following are methods of dry heat sterilisation except:
questions.explanation:
Autoclaving is a method of moist heat sterilization.
Dry heat sterilization | Moist heat sterilization
FlamingIncinerationHot air o ven | BoilingPasteurizationAutocla ving

questions.stem: What is the temperature that has to be maintained for sterilization in the device shown below? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
The image shown is a sterilizing hot air oven. The temperature to be maintained is 160° C for 2 hours.
Exposure to dry heat in a sterilizing hot air oven ensures the carbonization of organic material and the destruction of microorganisms and spores. The following combinations of temperature and duration of sterilization can be applied in hot air ovens:
180°C for 30 mins
170°C for 60 mins
160■C for 2 hours

questions.stem: An OT technician is sterilizing surgical instruments in the following device. What temperature should be maintained?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows an autoclave. Surgical instruments are sterilized at 121° C for 10-15 minutes.
Autoclaving is a form of moist heat sterilization which creates an increased temperature of steam under pressure. This method of sterilization is effective against spores also. Autoclaving is done for instruments that cannot withstand high temperatures of hot air oven or dry heat.

questions.stem: Which of the following materials are sterilized by a hot air oven?
questions.explanation: Glasswares, oils and powders, swabs, and dressings are sterilized by a hot air oven. Surgical instruments and culture media are sterilized by autoclave.

questions.stem: Šou have performed an upper GI endoscopy on a HbsAg positive patient. Which of the following should be used to sterilize the scope?
questions.explanation:
2% glutaraldehyde is used to sterilize endoscopes and fibreoptic scopes.
Aldehydes in 2% solutions (like glutaraldehyde and formaldehyde) have sporicidal activities. Glutaraldehyde is usually efficacious against tubercle bacteria, fungi & viruses.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false regarding the use of ethylene oxide in sterilisation and disinfection?
options: It is an inflammable and explosive gas
It is used for heat-sensitive objects
It is mixed with nitrogen for sterilization
questions.explanation:
A mixture of ethylene oxide with carbon dioxide is used for sterilization, not with nitrogen.
Ethylene oxide is an alkylating agent and has inflammable and explosive properties. It is often mixed with the following prior to use:
Carbon dioxide - decreases its explosive nature
Water vapor - increases the efficiency of the gas
Sterilization using this gas is usually done at 50-60 °C. and is suitable for heat-sensitive items like plastics, heart valves, dental equipment. It is effective against bacteria, spores, and some viruses.

questions.stem: The following machine was used during a cardiac bypass surgery. How is it best sterilized? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The image shown is a heart-lung machine. It is best sterilized using ethylene oxide.
Ethylene oxide gas diffuses through many types of porous materials and readily penetrates some plastics and is used for sterilizing machines.

questions.stem: Povidone - iodine is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Povidone - iodine is an iodophor.
Iodophors are iodine-based disinfectants in which iodine is combined with solubilizing agents or carriers. This results in the formation of a complex that provides a sustained release reservoir of iodine and releases small amounts of free iodine in an aqueous solution.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of precurrent disinfection?
options: Chlorination of a well by village public health authorities
Disinfection of kidney tray used during delivery of placenta
Disinfection of bed linen after the death of a patient
Disinfection of artery forceps following a surgery
questions.explanation:
Chlorination of water in a well is an example of precurrent disinfection.
Precurrent disinfection refers to prophylactic disinfection prior to discharge of infectious material. This includes pasteurization of milk, chlorination of water and hand washing.
Concurrent disinfection is the application of disinfection methods after discharge of infectious material from a person or soiling. This includes disinfection of urine, faeces, vomit, contaminated linen, clothes, hands.
Terminal disinfection is done after the death of a patient or transfer or after cessation of isolation.

questions.stem: Chlorine is the main disinfectant element in all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Cetrimide (trade name - Cetavlon) is a quaternary ammonia compound (QAC) that does not contain chlorine. QACs are low-level disinfectants and are sporostatic but not sporicidal. It is a bactericidal agent against vegetative gram-positive organisms.
Other QACs include cetrimide (cetavlon) and benzalkonium chloride.
Savlon contains cetrimide and chlorhexidine and is mainly used for plastic
items. Clinical thermometers may be best disinfected in Savlon mixed with spirit in a 1:6 ratio.
Chlorine compounds are potent disinfectants that are bactericidal, fungicidal, sporicidal, tuberculocidal, and virucidal.
Chlorine compounds | Mechanism of action and use s
1. Bleaching powder (chlorin ated lime) | Disinfection of water, feces, a nd urine
2. Chloramine - T | Has a prolonged bactericidal effect, used in a health care s etting
3. Hypochlorites | Disinfect infectious waste an d surfaces
4. Halazone tablets | Disinfect small quantities of water
5. Superoxidized water | Saline is electrolyzed to relea se hypochlorous acid and chl orine, which act as disinfecta nts

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide is:
questions.explanation:
Hydrogen peroxide is effective against bacteria, fungi, spores and viruses.
It is used in the hospital setting to disinfect surfaces. Sporicidal activities require higher concentrations and longer contact times. A 3% solution is also used as an antiseptic and for cleaning wounds and discharging ulcers.

questions.stem: Which among the following is a low-level disinfectant?
questions.explanation:
Benzalkonium chloride is a quaternary ammonium compound that is used as a low-level disinfectant.
There are 3 types of disinfectants:
Low-level disinfectant - kills only vegetative bacteria, fungi and lipid enveloped viruses (e.g.
quaternary ammonium compounds)
Intermediate level disinfectant: kills all microbes including mycobacteria and non-enveloped viruses, but not spores (e.g. alcohol, iodophors)
High-level disinfectant - This is a chemical that kills all microbial pathogens and some spores if the contact time is increased (e.g. glutaraldehyde, hydrogen peroxide)

questions.stem: Which among the following is not a sporicidal agent?
questions.explanation:
Cresol a phenolic compound is not sporicidal. Disinfectants that are not sporicidal are:
Biguanides
Alcohols
Heavy metal disinfectants
Organic acids
QACs
Phenolic compounds Sporicidal disinfectants include:
Aldehydes
Chlorine disinfectants
Hydrogen peroxide
Ethylene oxide
Peracetic acids

questions.stem: Which of the following disinfectants has anti-viral action?
questions.explanation:
Hypochlorite is an antiviral disinfectant. Antiviral disinfectants include:
Chlorine compounds
Phenol (at high concentrations)
Aldehydes
Hydrogen peroxide

questions.stem: A nurse in a PHC is using bleaching powder to disinfect bed linen contaminated with stool. What is the amount that she should use?
questions.explanation:
Bleaching powder of 50 g/L of water is required for disinfecting feces and urine. The agents commonly used for disinfecting faeces and urine are:
Disinfectant | Amount per lit re | Per ce nt
Bleaching pow der | 50 g | 5
Crude phenol | 100 ml | 10
Cresol | 50 ml | 5
Formalin | 100 ml | 10

questions.stem: Which of the following methods of disinfection is not effective against prions?
questions.explanation:
Benzalkonium chloride is not effective against prions. Prions can be inactivated by following the given steps:
Immersing the instruments in 1N NaOH or sodium hypochlorite for 1 hour
Then they are transferred to water
Then they are heated in a gravity displacement autoclave at 121°C for 1 hour
After this, they are cleaned and subjected to routine sterilization

questions.stem: Which of the following methods is not effective for disinfection of sputum of patients?
questions.explanation:
Chlorhexidine is not used to disinfect sputum. Sputum can be disinfected by:
Autoclaving or boiling - if a considerable amount of sputum is present (e.g. in TB hospitals)
5% cresol - patients are asked to spit in a sputum cup half-filled with cresol
Burning - for samples received in gauze or paper handkerchiefs

questions.stem: Match the following.
questions.explanation:
The biological indicators used to check the efficiency of various sterilization methods are:
Clostridium tetani - Hot air oven
Geobacillus stearothermophilus - Autoclave
Bacillus atrophaeus - Ethylene oxide
Bacillus pumilus - Ionizing radiation

questions.stem: Rideal-Walker co-efficient is employed for the assessment of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The Rideal-Walker coefficient helps in assessing the power of a disinfectant relative to phenol.
It assesses this by determining the phenol coefficient (PC). A PC value of > 1 indicates that it is more effective than phenol. The higher the number, the greater its effectiveness in comparison to phenol and vice versa. Traditional organisms used to test the power of the disinfectant
include S. aureus and Salmonella enteric subtype typhi.
Phenol coefficient = The dilution of test disinfectant which kills microorganisms in a given time ÷ The dilution of phenol which kills the microorganism in the same time under identical conditions.
Other tests that are used for disinfectants are as follows:
Chick Martin test - modification of the Rideal-Walker test where disinfectants act in the presence of organic matter like feces or yeast to simulate natural conditions
Kelsey-Skyes test (capacity test) - tests the capacity of a disinfectant to retain its activity when used repeatedly.
In-use test - determines whether the chosen disinfectant is effective in actual hospital use
Joseph Lister first introduced phenol (carbolic acid) as an antiseptic to sterilize surgical instruments and clean wounds. Lister's work led to a reduction in postoperative infections and made surgery safer for patients, distinguishing him as the 'Father of Modern Surgery' and 'Father of Antiseptic Surgery'.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false regarding the Spaulding classification?
options: Semi-critical items require high level disinfection
Non-critical items do not require disinfection
Cardiac catheters are classified as critical items
Critical items are associated with a high risk of infection
questions.explanation: Under the Spaulding classification, non-critical items require intermediate or low-level disinfection.

questions.stem: While collecting blood for samples, you have spilled some on the floor. What would be the immediate next step?
options: Call the infection control team of the hospital
questions.explanation:
The immediate next step in this scenario is to clean the spilled blood with absorbable material.
This absorbable material is then discarded in the yellow bin. Following this, sodium hypochlorite solution is used to decontaminate the surface. The concentrations of sodium hypochlorite used are:
< 10 mL blood spill - 1:100 dilution to decontaminate non-porous surfaces
> 10 mL blood spill or culture spill - 1:10 dilution for the first application, followed by 1:100 dilution

questions.stem: A blood spill in the operation theatre must be cleaned with .
questions.explanation:
Sodium hypochlorite, a compound of chlorine, is the best disinfectant for surface blood spills. It is used with a concentration of 0.5-5%.
If the spill contains large amounts of blood or body fluids, clean the visible matter with disposable absorbent material and discard the contaminated materials in appropriate, labelled containment.
A 1:10–1:100 dilution of 5.25%–6.15% sodium hypochlorite (i.e., household bleach) or an
EPA-registered tuberculocidal disinfectant has been recommended for decontaminating blood spills.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true for a screening test?
questions.explanation:
Screening tests are done on apparently healthy individuals, the results of the test are relatively inaccurate, the tests are based on one criterion.
The difference between screening and diagnostic tests is given below: Screening tests are recommended in the following conditions:
Early diagnosis changes the disease course
In a disease with an asymptomatic stage
In a disease with a test for diagnosis and treatment
The natural history of the disease is well known
Screening test | Diagnostic test
Done on apparently healthy | Done on patients with signs a nd symptoms
Applied to groups | Applied to single patients
Based on one criterion or cut -off point | Based on evaluation of a num ber of symptoms, signs, and l aboratory findings
Less accurate | More accurate
Less expensive | More expensive
Not a basis for treatment | Used as a basis for treatment
The initiative comes from the investigator or agency provi ding care | The initiative comes from a p atient with a complaint

questions.stem: Below is a diagram depicting the natural history of the disease. Which point marks the onset of symptoms? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
Point C represents a point where signs and symptoms appear. Various points marked in the image represent the following:
Point A: Entry of infectious agent into the host.
Point B: Pathological and physiological changes occur in the stage of the subclinical phase. These changes are induced by the causative agent but are not sufficient enough to cause clinical signs and symptoms.
Point C: Marks onset of clinical signs and symptoms.
Point D: Usual time of diagnosis at which clinical signs and symptoms are well evident.
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: In the following natural history of disease flowchart, point A to C is called as? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
Lead time is the period between the first possible time of detection (point A) and the usual time of diagnosis (point C).
Screening time is the time difference between the first point of diagnosis and the critical point of diagnosis.
Diagnosis of a disease before the critical point has a good outcome and reduces the severity by reversing the disease process. Diagnosis beyond the critical point treatment would be unsuccessful and/or permanent damage would have occurred.
Screening must be done in conditions where there is a considerable time lag between the onset of disease and the usual time of diagnosis. That is conditions with a long lead time.
Generation time is defined as the interval of time between the onset of infection by a host and the maximal infectivity of that host.

questions.stem: In which of the following diseases, screening procedure increases the overall survival to the maximum?
questions.explanation:
Screening of colon cancer increases the overall survival to the maximum.
Colon cancer has a long lead time and can be detected early before pathological changes occur. It can be curable if treated early, otherwise fatal in half the cases.
Early diagnosis and treatment before the critical point have a good outcome and reduce the severity by reversing the disease process. Diagnosis beyond the critical point treatment would be unsuccessful and/or permanent damage would have occurred.
Other diseases that can be screened are:
Cervical cancer
Breast cancer
Prostate cancer

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of prospective screening?
options: Cervical Pap smear in a 40 year old patient
Neonatal screening of a new-born baby for hypothyroidism
Screening of immigrants to a country
Urine for sugar screening in a 40 year old man
questions.explanation:
Screening of immigrants to a country is an example of prospective screening.
Screening of disease is done to detect unrecognized disease or defect, in apparently healthy individuals, by means of rapidly applied tests, examinations, or other procedures.
The difference between prospective and prescriptive screening is given below:
Note: Most common neonatal disease to be screened for is neonatal hypothyroidism.
 | Prospective screening | Prescriptive screening
Definition | People screened for others be nefit | People screened solely for the ir own benefit

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most important factor in reduction of diphtheria cases?
questions.explanation: Vaccination is the most important factor responsible for the reduction of diphtheria cases over the past decade.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about pertussis?
options: Most of the infections are subclinical
Secondary attack rate is 90 % in unimmunized individuals
Cerebellar ataxia is a common chronic complication
questions.explanation:
The secondary attack rate in pertussis is about 90% in unimmunized individuals.
The source of infection in pertussis is a case of pertussis. There is no evidence of subclinical infections. The patients are most infectious during the catarrhal stage.
The chief complications of pertussis are:
Bronchopneumonia
Bronchitis
Bronchiectasis

questions.stem: Droplet precaution and isolation is to be done for all of the following conditions except:
questions.explanation:
Droplet precaution and isolation is not done for localized varicella zoster, as it is only transmitted through direct contact.
Varicella-zoster localized in the patient with an intact immune system with a lesion that can be contained/covered do not require droplet precaution. Disseminated varicella in any patient requires airborne and contact precautions.
Diphtheria, pertussis, and mycoplasma are transmitted by droplets and hence require droplet precaution and isolation.
Although patients are not contagious starting 48 hours after antibiotic therapy, droplet precautions are typically maintained until the completion of the antibiotic course and are culture-negative on two cultures taken 24 hours apart. Droplet precautions include the use of masks, gowns, gloves and protective eye gear when providing direct patient care.

questions.stem: A polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae has 23 serotypes. In which of the following patients is this vaccine most beneficial?
options: A patient with sickle cell disease
A patient with recurrent otitis media
questions.explanation:
The polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae (PPSV-23) is most beneficial for patients with sickle cell disease.
S. pneumoniae is an encapsulated organism that is detected by the spleen and is removed. However, in sickle cell disease, the sickled cells block the vessels in the spleen which results in splenic infarction. This hyposplenism results in an increased risk of pneumococcal infection. Hence, pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV-23) is given to these patients as a prophylactic measure to reduce this risk.

questions.stem: Which of the following tests is used to determine the prevalence of TB infection?
questions.explanation:
Mantoux or tuberculin testing is used to detect the prevalence of TB infection.
238
Infection of tuberculosis does not always lead to disease. In latent infections, the Mantoux test can be positive without any clinical symptoms. Therefore, the prevalence of TB infection is detected by the Mantoux test.
However, the prevalence of TB disease is confirmed by a sputum smear.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old patient has been given an intradermal injection of 0.1ml PPD (5 tuberculin units) over the forearm. After 72 hrs, the site is examined as shown in the image below. What is the interpretation of the result obtained? [[IMG:1]]
options: Tuberculin test negative, suggesting immunity from TB
Tuberculin test positive, suggesting an active infection
Tuberculin test negative, suggesting a recent or past infection
Tuberculin test positive, suggesting a recent or past infection
questions.explanation:
The above image shows an induration of >10 mm after 72 hrs of intradermal PPD injection suggesting a positive tuberculin test(TST), indicating recent or past infection.
In TST, 0.1 ml of PPD (purified protein derivative) containing 5 TU (tuberculosis unit) is injected intradermally and induration is read after 48-72 hours. An induration of 10 mm or more is considered positive in patients from countries with a high prevalence of tuberculosis. Surrounding erythema is not considered.
A positive tuberculin test indicates hypersensitivity to tuberculoprotein, denoting either latent infection with tubercle bacilli, or BCG immunization, or recent or past infection with or without clinical disease.
False positives may be seen in infections with related mycobacteria and false negatives in miliary tuberculosis, severely immunosuppressed states, etc.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate method to assess the incidence of tuberculosis in the community?
options: Identify all positives to tuberculin test
Identify new converter to tuberculin test
Screen all under 5 years children with tuberculin test
questions.explanation:
Identification of new converters to the tuberculin test is a marker of the incidence of tuberculosis. Identification of all positives to the tuberculin test is a marker of the prevalence of tuberculosis.
Tuberculin conversion refers to the situation where an individual’s tuberculin skin test (TST) results in changes from negative (0–4 mm diameter induration) to positive (equal to or >10 mm diameter induration) within a 24-month period. TST conversion is considered presumptive evidence of acquired latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) and potential risk for progression to active tuberculosis disease.

questions.stem: Tuberculin testing is done at which anatomical site?
questions.explanation:
Mantoux/ Tuberculin testing is carried out by injecting 1 TU of PPD in 0.1 ml intradermally on the flexor (ventral) surface of the left forearm, midway between elbow and wrist.
The result of the test is usually read after 48-96 hours, but reading it after 72 hours is ideal.
The horizontal transverse diameter of induration is measured, based on which the following diagnosis can be inferred:
< 6 mm – Negative
6–9 mm – Doubtful
 10 mm – Positive

questions.stem: The approach shown in the image is a part of which of the following? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
questions.explanation:
Detect – Treat – Prevent – Build approach for eliminating TB in India is part of the National Strategic Plan for TB (2017-2025). The components of this approach are:
Detect - Early identification of presumptive TB cases, at the first point of care, be it private or public sectors, and prompt diagnosis using high sensitivity diagnostic tests.
Treat - Provide sustained, equitable access to high quality TB treatment, care and support services.
Prevent - Prevent the emergence of TB in susceptible populations.
Build - Undertake critical management reforms, restructuring of HR and financial norms, pathways for private sector participation, in order to improve efficiency, effectiveness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most rapid diagnostic test for pulmonary TB? 231
questions.explanation:
The most rapid diagnosis of pulmonary TB can be done by sputum microscopy, with results in 30 minutes.
It has the least sensitivity and specificity. Smears are stained by Ziel Neelson acid-fast stain.
CBNAAT gives results within 90 minutes. Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test is a Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific automated, cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification assay, having fully integrated and automated amplification and detection using real-time PCR.
Quantiferon TB gold plus takes 24 hours to give the result. The radiometric BACTEC method takes approximately 2-3 weeks. Sputum culture takes approximately 2 to 8 weeks.

questions.stem: BCG vaccine provides protection against which of the following?
questions.explanation:
BCG vaccine provides protection against CNS and disseminated TB.
It does not prevent primary infection. More importantly, it does not prevent reactivation of latent pulmonary infection, the principal source of bacillary spread in the community. The impact of BCG vaccination on transmission of mycobacterium tuberculosis is therefore limited.

questions.stem: What is the next step in management of a TB smear positive patient with no significant findings on a chest X ray?
questions.explanation:
The next best step in a smear-positive patient with no findings on chest-xray is to perform a CB-NAAT. This patient is a microscopically confirmed case of tuberculosis (TB).
According to the TB annual report, CBNAAT has been tried to be established in all centres. Ideally, drug sensitivity status via NAAT is to be done following a sputum smear before initiation of treatment. This helps in the early detection and treatment of drug-resistant TB. This has been integrated into the regular TB services to detect rifampicin resistance at the time of diagnosis.
Depending on the sensitivity of the tubercle bacilli, appropriate ATT is started.
If NAAT is not done and sputum is positive, patient is considered as Microbiologically positive with sensitivity status unknown.

Duration of ATT in TB meningitis is for 9 months and lymph node and abdominal TB is 6 months.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of disability limitation for polio?
options: Polio immunization drives for infants to reduce the occurence.
Arranging for schooling for a child suffering from residual polio paralysis.
Resting the limbs affected by polio in neutral position.
Providing calipers for walking to patients affected by polio.
questions.explanation:
Resting the limbs affected by polio in a neutral position is an example of disability limitation. It is an intervention done to either halt or prevent the transition of the disease process from impairment to handicap.
Rehabilitation has been defined as the use of medical, social, educational, and vocational measures for training the individual to the highest possible level of functional ability. Like providing calipers for walking to patients and arranging schooling after being affected by polio.
Immunization drives are examples of specific protection.

questions.stem: A person is involved in unsafe sexual practices. Which of the following viruses is least likely to get transmitted via this route?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis E has feco-oral or waterborne transmission. It does not transmit sexually. Transmission of Hepatitis A, C, and D can occur sexually.
Transmission of the hepatitis A virus can occur from any sexual activity with an infected person and is not limited to fecal-oral contact. People who are sexually active are considered at risk for hepatitis A if they are MSM, live with or are having sex with an infected person, or inject drugs.

questions.stem: For how long is Hepatitis A excreted in the feces?
options: One week before the symptoms appear
Two weeks after the symptoms appear
Two weeks before the symptoms and two weeks thereafter
One week before the symptoms and one week thereafter
questions.explanation:
HAV is excreted in the feces for about 2 weeks before the onset of jaundice and for up to 2 weeks thereafter.
The risk of transmitting is greatest at 2 weeks before to 1 week after the onset of jaundice.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman is rushed to the hospital with labor pains at 34 weeks of gestation. She did not attend any prior antenatal visits. On further evaluation, she is found to be positive for HbsAg. Which of the following should be administered to the newborn after delivery?

HBIG does not interfere with the antibody response to the hepatitis B vaccine. This combined procedure is ideal both for postexposure prophylaxis of persons accidentally exposed to blood known to contain hepatitis B virus and for the prevention of the carrier state in the newborn babies of carrier mothers.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about Rotavirus?
options: Severe rotavirus infections are limited to children aged 5-7 years.
Rotavirus is shed in high concentrations for several days in the stools and vomit of infected children.
Rotavirus diarrhoea increases in frequency during drier, cooler months.
Clean water supplies and good hygiene are unlikely to have a substantial effect on viral transmission.
questions.explanation:
Severe rotavirus gastroenteritis is largely limited to children aged 6-24 months, not 5-7 years.
Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhea in children aged <5 years globally. In developing countries, 75% of the children acquire their first rotavirus infection in the first 12 months.
The universal occurrence of rotavirus infections shows that clean water supply and good hygiene are unlikely to have a substantial effect on virus transmission. In tropical areas, rotavirus diarrhea occurs throughout the year, increasing in frequency in drier, cooler climates.
Transmission is through the feco-oral route, person-to-person contact, or indirectly through fomites. Infected individuals shed very high concentrations of the virus for many days in their stool and vomit.

Rotavirus vaccines are live, attenuated, and are administered orally. So, it is not given to an immunocompromised child.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false for carriers of cholera?
options: A convalescent carrier may continue to excrete vibrios for 2-3 weeks.
The gall bladder is infected in chronic carriers.
The antibody titres of a contact carrier is normal while the stool culture is positive.
questions.explanation:
The antibody titers of all carriers are risen and positive till the person harbors the organism. A cholera carrier is defined as an apparently healthy person excreting V.cholerae O1 in stools.
Selective media and enrichment is needed for their diagnosis. In cholera, 4 types of carriers are described.
Incubatory/Pre-Clinical carriers: The duration of carrier state is 1-5 days (incubation period). They present with symptoms later.
Convalescent carriers: Recovered from an attack of cholera, continues to excrete vibrios for 2-3 weeks, due to ineffective antibiotic treatment.
Contact/Health carrier: Due to subclinical infection contracted through a case or an infected environment, may excrete for 10 days.
Chronic carriers: Gallbladder is infected, duration may be as long as 10 years.

questions.stem: A convalescent carrier of cholera will remain infectious for how many days after recovery?
questions.explanation:
A convalescent carrier of cholera will remain infectious for 14-21 days after recovery.
This type of carrier continues to excrete vibrios after being recovered from an attack of cholera. It is seen due to ineffective antibiotic treatment. These carriers can often become chronic or
long-term carriers.

options: A cardiotonic should be added if shock persists even after treating with iv fluids.
If the diarrhoea persists after 48 hours of treatment, suspect resistance.
Antidiarrheals and antiemetics should be started.
questions.explanation:
In patients with cholera, if diarrhea persists after 48 hours of antibiotic therapy, resistance to the antibiotic should be suspected.
Treatment for cholera:
Rehydration therapy - is started immediately, either oral or intravenous.
Antibiotic therapy - As soon as vomiting has stopped (usually after 3-4 hours of rehydration). Fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, azithromycin, ampicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are commonly used.
Shock in diarrhea must be corrected by intravenous fluids only.
Antidiarrhoeals, cardiotonics, antiemetics, antispasmodics, and corticosteroids are not used.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man is diagnosed with cholera. Which of the following drug would you prescribe to his family members to prevent the spread of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Tetracycline is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of cholera. It should be given for:
Adults - a 3-day period in a twice-daily dose of 500mg
Children (4-13 years) - 125mg
Children (0-3 years) - 50mg
Alternatively, the long-acting tetracycline (doxycycline) may be used for chemoprophylaxis, if the prevailing strains are not resistant. A single oral dose of doxycycline (300 mg for adults and 6 mg/kg for children under 15 years) has proved to be effective.
Chemoprophylaxis is advised only for household contacts or a closed community in which cholera has occurred.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most effective prophylactic measure against cholera?
questions.explanation:
The most important effective measure against cholera is health education. The prophylactic measures against cholera include:
Health education
Food hygiene practices
Hand washing practices after defecation
Drinking safe water
Knowledge about ORS

questions.stem: You are a medical officer posted in a village 'X'. The village has been affected by the epidemic of cholera. What is the first step that should be taken to decrease the incidence of the disease?
options: Cholera vaccination to all uninfected individuals
Treat everyone in the village with tetracycline
questions.explanation:
Safe water supply and sanitation is the first step to be taken to decrease the incidence of cholera. Steps taken to decrease the incidence of cholera include:
Safe water supply
Excreta disposal
Food sanitation
Disinfection
Early case detection
Cholera Vaccines: available in oral forms
Dukoral
Sanchol and mORCVAX
Euvichol
Vaxchora
CVD103-HgR - no longer produced
Sanchol and Euvichol are available for mass vaccination campaigns. The campaigns have been implemented in areas experiencing an outbreak, in areas at heightened vulnerability during humanitarian crises, and among populations living in highly endemic areas, known as hotspots.
Vaxchora is given for adults (18 – 64 years) who are traveling to an area of active cholera transmission, at least 10 days before the trip.
Mass chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for the control of cholera. This is because the drug's effect is only short-lived (a few days). Moreover, for preventing 1 case of cholera, around 10,000 individuals must be given the drug. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for only household contacts of confirmed cases with tetracycline.

questions.stem: In the ward, a patient with cholera soils the bed with stools. Which chemical should be used to disinfect the bed?
questions.explanation:
The most effective disinfectant for cholera stool is a coal tar disinfectant with Riedel-Walker (RW)
coefficient of >10 such as cresol. Bleaching powder, if used, should be of good quality.
For disinfection, attention should be paid to the following: patient's stools and vomit; clothes and other contaminated personal items; the latrine, the patient's house, and neighborhood.

questions.stem: Cholera is a notifiable disease locally and nationally. Which of the following statements is true regarding the international health regulations for the notification of Cholera?
options: Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 72 hours of its occurence.
The number of cases and deaths are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.
An area is declared free of cholera when 1 month has elapsed since the last case.
Mass chemoprophylaxis must be initiated immediately.
questions.explanation:
The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.
International health regulations for the notification of Cholera:
Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 24 hours of its occurrence.
The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.
When twice the incubation period (5 days) i.e. 10 days has elapsed since the death, recovery, or isolation of the last case, an area is declared free of cholera.
Mass prophylaxis is not advised in cholera, as it fails to stop the spread of the disease. Chemoprophylaxis is only advised for household contacts or a closed community.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has had 15 episodes of loose stools in the last 24 hours and vomited twice in the last 4 hours. The child is restless and has sunken eyes. On examination, he is irritable but is drinking fluids. What is the optimal therapy for the child?
options: Intravenous fluid initially for 4 hours followed by oral fluids
questions.explanation:
Oral rehydration therapy is the optimal therapy to treat acute diarrheas in some dehydration patients.
Recommended formulation: Reduced osmolarity ORS solution, which has a reduced concentration of sodium (75 mmol/liter) and glucose (75 mmol/liter). It helps in reducing the adverse effect of hypertonicity on net fluid absorption.
According to IMNCI guidelines, irritable child who is able to drink fluids come under some dehydration category.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: A mother brings her child with complaints of acute diarrhea. After an initial assessment, you diagnose that the child has some dehydration. You counsel the mother to give ORS. After how many hours shall she be advised to discard the old solution and prepare a new one?
questions.explanation:
The freshly prepared ORS should not be used after 24 hours. Guidelines for administering ORS:
After each loose stool, give:
Children <2 years of age - 50-100 ml (a quarter to half a large cup) of fluid
Children 2 to 10 years - 100-200 ml (a half to one large cup)
Older children and adults - as much fluid as they want
For children <2 years, give a teaspoon every 1 to 2 minutes and offer frequent sips out of a cup for older children. Try to give the estimated required amount within a 4-hour period.
If the child vomits, wait for 10 minutes, then give a spoonful every 2 to 3 minutes.
If the child wants to drink more ORS solution than the estimated amount and does not vomit, there is no harm in feeding him/her more.
If the child is breastfeeding, continue breastfeeding with ORS solution.

questions.stem: A baby is brought with complaints of diarrhea and vomiting. The weight of the baby is 12 kgs. What is the estimated amount of fluid to be replaced in 4 hours?
questions.explanation:
According to the guidelines of ORS by WHO, a child with a weight of 11-15.˜ kg has to be treated with 800-1200 ml of ORS solution within the first 4 hours.
Guidelines for oral rehydration therapy (for all ages) during the first four hours by WHO: The patient's age should be used if weight is not known.
The approximate amount of ORS required in ml may also be calculated by 75 x body weight (kg).
Age | Under 4 mo nths | 4-11 mon ths | 1-2 y rs | 2-4yrs | 5-14 yr s | 15 yrs or ove r
Weight (kg) | under 5 | 5-7.˜ | 8-10. ˜ | 11-15. ˜ | 16-2˜.˜ | 30 or over
ORS solution ( ml) | 200-400 | 400-600 | 600- 800 | 800-1 200 | 1200-2 200 | 2200-4000

questions.stem: A ˜-month-old baby with diarrhea is feeding well and is thirsty. Skin pinch when done returns in 2 seconds. What is the treatment?
options: 200-400 ml of ORS to be given in the first four hours.
400-700 ml of ORS to be given in the first four hours.
700-˜00 ml of ORS to be given in the first 4 hours.
In addition to the usual fluid intake, 100-200 ml should be given after each loose stool.
questions.explanation:
According to the IMNCI classification, the baby has some dehydration and comes under Plan B. The amount of ORS given is 75ml/kg body weight.
Here, the weight of the child is not specified. Hence, 400-700 ml of ORS at home is to be given in the first four hours according to the age of the child. The below table shows the amount of ORS to be given according to the age of the child.
In addition to this, 50-100 ml extra fluid is given after each loose stool. After four hours, the baby is reassessed and the appropriate plan is selected again for the continuation of the treatment.
The four rules of home treatment are:
Give extra fluid
Give zinc supplements (1 tablet per day for 14 days, dissolved in a small amount of ORS or breast milk or clean water)
Continue breastfeeding
Counsel the mother to return if there is blood in stools and if the child is feeding poorly
