questions.explanation: The Uday Pareek scale is used for the classification of socio-economic status in rural areas.

questions.stem: Which of the following components are included under the modified ‘uppuswamy scale for socio-economic status ?
questions.explanation: The modified ‘uppuswamy scale uses income of the family, education and occupation of head of family.

questions.stem: Match the following scores in accordance with Modified ‘uppuswamy’s scale.
questions.explanation:
The correct match is 1-d, 2-b, 3-a, 4-c.
Socioeconomic class according to Modified ‘uppuswamy Scale:
Socioeconomic cla ss | Scor es
Upper | 25-2 9
Upper Middle | 16-2 5
Lower Middle | 11-15
Socioeconomic cla ss | Scor es
Upper Lower | 05-1 0
Lower | 01-0 4

questions.stem: In the doctor-patient relationship, which of the following is not a level of communication?
questions.explanation:
Communication on a psychological plane is not a level of communication in a doctor-patient relationship.
For a successful doctor-patient relationship, a doctor must have in his/her regard communication on the following levels:
Communication on an emotional plane: To build rapport, ensure openness and incite trust from the patient.
Communication on a cultural plane: To understand the community to which the patient belongs, his/her cultural factors that may influence health and disease and also for economic understanding of the patient.
Communication on an intellectual plane: To give adequate explanation for their conditions and help the patients develop insight into their ailments.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best suited role for a medical social worker?
options: Designing coping strategies, interviewing and case work
questions.explanation:
A medical social worker is a person who is trained mainly in social work and interviewing.
He/she carries out duties that augment public and community healthcare by way of identifying, understanding and relaying important information about a patient’s determinants of health.
They are not involved in active treatment, prescribing or providing economic support.

questions.stem: Which of the following practices is covered under the COPRA act?
questions.explanation:
Consumer Protection Act or COPRA was instituted in 1986 and deals with consumer rights. It recognizes six rights of the consumers, which are:
Right to safety
Right to be informed
Right to be heard
Right to choose
Right to seek redressal
Right to consumer education

questions.stem: Which of the following is used to describe an interview used to note the gradual influence of some social or psychological process?
questions.explanation:
A repetitive interview is used to note the gradual influence of some social or psychological process. A record is maintained to understand the changes.
Interviews are methods used widely in investigations and in research. A proper interview technique must be employed to achieve the objective.
Aims of an interview:
To secure information usually through face to face association and to understand the individual/group being interviewed.
To form a hypothesis.
To collect personal data for quantitative purposes.
To collect data from secondary sources of information. Types of interviews:
A direct or structured interview consists of predetermined questions and sequence.
A non-directive or unstructured interview doesn’t have any sequence of questions set beforehand. The interviewer listens and allows the speaker to narrate his/her own experiences or opinions.
A focused interview is usually used to study effects of mass communication like radio broadcasts or film. In this, the interviewer/researcher focuses on a particular aspect on the problem and draws responses from people.
A repetitive interview is used to note the gradual influence of some social or psychological process. A record is maintained to understand the changes.

questions.stem: Arrange the following steps of an interview in the correct order in a sequence.
options: Starting an interview, making a report, establishing contact, securing rapport
Establishing contact, making a report, starting an interview, securing rapport
Establishing contact, starting an interview, securing rapport, making a report
Starting an interview, securing rapport, making a report, establishing contact
questions.explanation:
The correct sequence of steps of interviewing are establishing contact, starting an interview, securing rapport, making a report.
Technique of interviewing involves:
Establishing contact
Starting an interview
Securing rapport
Recall
Probe questions
Encouragement
Guiding the interview
Recording
Closing the interview
Report

questions.stem: What is the application of scientific methods to investigate the study of complex human organizations, services and management called?
questions.explanation:
Operational research is the application of scientific methods of investigation to study complex human organizations, services and management.
Pure research is also called fundamental research or basic research. It is aimed at improving scientific theories or understanding of them.
Applied research is a methodology used for a specific, practical problem like diseases or business. It involves the practical application of science.

questions.stem: What was the purpose of setting up the Nirbhaya Fund?
options: Providing free medical care for women
questions.explanation: The Nirbhaya Fund was set up by the government of India for promoting the safety of women.

questions.stem: Choose the correct match.
options: Gross Domestic Product- gross income generated only from within the country
Gross National Product- gross domestic product minus the depreciation on a country’s capital goods
Net National Product- income generated from within the country and income received from abroad
Net Domestic Product- market value of all final goods and services in a country during a year after allowing for depreciation
questions.explanation: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the income generated only from within the country and does not include income received from abroad.

questions.stem: What percentage of GDP was spent on public health in 2020?
questions.explanation:
The total public health expenditure is around 1.25% percentage of India's GDP (National Health Profile 2020 report).
The National Health Policy, 2017 states the aim to increase this to around 2.5% by 2025.

questions.stem: A mother brings her 4-year-old boy for a well-baby check-up. Upon examination the paediatrician diagnoses her son with hidden hunger. What is meant by the term hidden hunger?
options: Child's diet is deficient in carbohydrates
Child is taking a diet that is deficient in essential amino acids
Child suffers from deficiency of omega 3 fatty acids
questions.explanation:
Hidden hunger refers to micronutrient deficiency. It occurs when there is deficiency in intake or absorption of micronutrients like vitamins, iron, zinc, etc.
The health effects of these deficiencies are less obvious or invisible and thus referred to as hidden hunger. The consequences of hidden hunger are seen in all ages.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct with regards to the estimation of poverty line?
options: Per capita expenditure of Rs. 32 per day in urban areas
Per capita expenditure of Rs. 47 per day in rural areas
Daily calorie intake of 2100 calories in urban areas
Daily calorie intake of 2700 calories in rural areas
questions.explanation:
An estimate of the poverty line is the expenditure required for a daily calorie intake of 2100 in urban areas and 2400 in rural areas, per person.
Income-based poverty line in India is per capita expenditure of Rs. 47 in urban areas and Rs. 32 in rural areas per day.

questions.stem: Which of the following legislations does not offer social security for industrial workers?
questions.explanation:
The Labour Charter Act does not offer social security for industrial workers.
Social security is the security that society furnishes through appropriate organization, against certain risks to which its members are exposed. These risks include sickness, maternity, old age and death.
Social security for industrial workers is given by:
Workmen’s Compensation Act
The Family Pension Scheme
Central Maternity Benefit Act
Employees’ State Insurance Act
Social security for civil servants is given by governments in the form of pension, gratuity, provident fund, etc. The Central Government Health Scheme provides security to employees of the Central Government.
Insurance schemes from the likes of Life Insurance Corporation of India, etc. have security schemes for the general public.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a component of the global hunger index (GHI)?
options: Percentage of undernourished children under 5 years
questions.explanation:
The infant mortality rate is not a component of the global hunger index.
The Global Hunger Index (GHI) has three dimensions. These dimensions are measured by indicators.
GHI score = (1/3 X standardized PUN) + (1/6 X standardised CWA) + (1/6 X standardised CST) + (1/3 X Standardised CM)
Where,
PUN is the proportion of the population that is undernourished
CWA is the prevalence of wasting in children under 5 years of age
CST is the prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age
CM is the proportion of children dying under the age of 5 years of age.
The result lies on a scale from 0 to 100, with 0 meaning no hunger and 100 being the worst score. The GHI is given by the International Food Policy Research Institute. In 2021, India's GHI was
27.5. It ranks 101 among 116 countries. In the 2022,India's GHI stands at 29.1, and India ranks 107th out of the 121 countries.
Dimensions | Indicators
Inadequate food supp ly | Proportion of the population undernourished
Child mortality | Under 5 mortality rate
Child undernutrition | Wasting in children under 5 yearsStunting in children un der 5 years

chapters.title: Water - I: Sources and purification of water

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a component of the definition of safe and wholesome water?
questions.explanation:
Water intended for human consumption must be safe and wholesome. It must be colorless. Safe and wholesome water is defined as:
Free from pathogenic agents
Free from harmful chemicals
Pleasant to taste, free from colour and odour
Usable for domestic purposes
Water is said to be polluted when it does not fulfill the above criteria.

questions.stem: In an urban PHC, an increasing number of skin diseases are being reported due to inadequate water supply in the region. What would be the adequate supply of water for them to meet their needs for all domestic purposes?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario of skin diseases is suggestive of water-washed diseases caused by improper hygiene related to an inadequate water supply. In urban areas, 150–200 litres per capita per day is the recommended allowance to meet the needs for all kinds of domestic purposes.
In rural areas, the set target of water supply to be achieved in India is around 50-55 litres per capita per day.

questions.stem: What are the norms for the required litres of water per capita per day in rural areas?
questions.explanation:
According to the National Rural Drinking Water Programme, the requirement of water in rural areas (areas with public water posts) is 55 litres per capita per day. This is in accordance with the 12th Five Year Plan.
For reasons of comparability, the source of water provision in rural areas should be within a distance of 100 metres from the household or the time taken to fetch water should not be > 30 minutes.
Note: Park textbook mentions 40-50 litres per capita per day as the norm. However, in the 12th five year plan period, the Government of India enhanced the rural drinking water supply norms from 40 litres to 55 litres per capita per day.

questions.stem: What is the purest form of water in nature?
questions.explanation:
Rain water is the purest form of water in nature. It contains a very low amount of total dissolved solids (TDS). Rain water is the origin of both surface and ground water.
Sources of water:
Rain
Surface water:
Impounding reservoirs
Rivers and streams
Tanks, ponds and lakes
Ground water:
Shallow wells
Deep wells
Springs

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a source of surface water?
questions.explanation:
Shallow wells are sources of ground water. Sources of water:
Rain
Surface water:
Impounding reservoirs
Rivers and streams
Tanks, ponds and lakes
Ground water:
Shallow wells
Deep wells
Springs

questions.stem: What is the area from which water drains into impounding reservoirs known as?
questions.explanation:
The area draining into the impounding reservoirs are known as catchment areas.
Impounding reservoirs are also called embankment ponds. These reservoirs are artificial lake-like water bodies. They are made by building an embankment or earth fill in an area into which natural water flows and can be stored for usage. Dams are also built to create these reservoirs.
Water from these reservoirs is second in purity to rainwater but is not completely free from impurities. Catchment areas are the main sources of impurities in the water in impounding
reservoirs.
The image given below shows catchment area:
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: What is the most common type of well in India?
questions.explanation: Dug wells are the most common type of wells in India.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about artesian wells?
options: It is not common in India
Water is put under pressure between two impervious layers
No pump is required to bring water to surface
It is a type of shallow well
questions.explanation: Artesian wells are types of deep wells.

questions.stem: Step wells belong to which of the following types of wells?
questions.explanation: Step wells belong to the type of pucca dug wells.

questions.stem: An outbreak of guinea worm disease was reported among villagers who used step wells for drinking water. In order to arrest the spread of disease, a decision was made to replace step wells with sanitary and safe wells. All of the following measures would be considered during its construction except:
options: Must be located at least 15 metres away from sources of contamination
A partition space for washing clothes and vessels
Lining must be made to a depth of 6 metres or more
Hand-pump must be made to handle rough use
questions.explanation:
Washing clothes, vessels, and bathing must be prohibited around wells to avoid contamination of the water.
Step wells are a type of pucca wells which enable people to descend into the well to fetch water. It is obsolete now, as there is considerable personal contact between the user and the water which can pose a health hazard to the community.

questions.stem: What is the minimum length that the platform of a well should extend around it in all directions?
questions.explanation: The platform of a sanitary well should stretch for at least 1 metre around the well in all directions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a water-washed disease?
questions.explanation:
Cholera is a water-borne disease and not a water-washed disease.
The diseases which are transmitted by improper hygiene and are widely related to circumstances where there is inadequate water supply are called water-washed diseases.
Some examples of water-washed diseases are:
Conjunctivitis
Trachoma
Scabies
Typhus

questions.stem: A multipurpose worker is spraying herbicides on aquatic plants as part of vector control measures in your area. Which of the following water-related diseases can be controlled by this approach?
questions.explanation:
Filariasis (caused by B.malayi) is transmitted by Mansonia species of mosquito that breeds in water bodies containing aquatic vegetation. It can be controlled by the use of herbicides to destroy aquatic vegetation.
Water-related diseases are classified as:
Category | Examples
Water-borne diseases | Caused by ingestion of water contaminated by human or a nimal faeces, or urine contai ning pathogenic bacteria or v iruses.ex: Cholera, typhoid, a moebic and bacillary dysente ry, and other diarrhoeal disea ses.
Water-washed diseases | Caused by poor personal hygi ene.ex: Scabies, trachoma, fle a-, lice- and tick-borne diseas es, in addition to the majorit y of waterborne diseases (whi ch are also water-washed).
Water-based diseases | Caused by parasites found in intermediate organisms livin g in water.ex: Dracunculiasis, schistosomiasis and some ot her helminths.
Category	Examples | Category	Examples
Water-related diseases trans mitted by insect vectors | Caused by vectors that breed in waterex: Dengue, filariasis, malaria, onchocerciasis, tryp anosomiasis and yellow fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods of purification of water cannot be used on a large scale?
questions.explanation: Berkefeld filter is used for the purification of water on a small scale (ex: in households).

questions.stem: During your posting as a rural medical officer, you conduct an awareness drive prior to the monsoon season in order to highlight the necessity of water purification. Which of the following methods would you not recommend for a household setup?
questions.explanation: Slow sand filter is a method of filtration used for the purification of water on a large scale.

questions.stem: When river water is stored properly, by how much percent does the bacterial count drop in the first 5-7 days?
questions.explanation:
When river water is stored properly, the bacterial count drops by as much as 90% in the first 5 – 7 days.
Purification during the storage of water is a natural process that takes place by physical, chemical and biological phenomena. Components of water purification include storage, filtration and disinfection.

questions.stem: What is the other name for slow sand filters?
questions.explanation: Slow sand filters are also called biological filters.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a part of a slow sand filter?
questions.explanation:
Components of a slow sand filter include:
Under-drainage system
Sand bed and a layer of organic matter
Filter control system
Supernatant water
Filter box

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about slow sand filters?
options: The thickness of sand bed is 2 metres
It takes a longer duration for water purification
The sand grain size is 0.4 to 0.7 mm
questions.explanation: Slow sand filters take a longer duration than most other methods for purification of water.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Schmutzdecke?
options: Layer of alum flocculate on supernatant water
Layer of algae and diatoms on supernatant water
Layer of alum flocculate on surface of sand bed filter
Layer of algae and diatoms on surface of sand bed filter
questions.explanation: Schmutzdecke refers to the vital layer which is formed by algae, plankton, diatoms and bacteria on the surface of the sand bed filter.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not the vital layer of a slow sand filter?
questions.explanation: The vital layer of a slow sand filter is also called the zoogleal layer, Schmutzdecke, or the biological layer.

questions.stem: Where is the vital layer of the slow sand filter seen?
options: On top of the raw water
questions.explanation: The vital layer of the slow sand filter is seen on the sand bed.

questions.stem: What does the venturi meter measure in a slow sand filter?
questions.explanation:
Venturi meters measure the bed resistance or loss of head in a slow sand filter. The following image shows a venturi meter:
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following is an incorrect statement about rapid sand filters?
options: No preliminary storage of raw water is required
Can be gravity or pressure type
questions.explanation: Frequent washing of the filter bed is required in rapid sand filters. This is done by backwashing.

questions.stem: What is the effective size of sand grains in a rapid sand filter?
questions.explanation: Effective size of sand grains in a rapid sand filter is 0.4 – 0.7 mm. Effective size of sand grains in a slow sand filter is 0.2 – 0.3 mm.

questions.stem: Rapid sand filter is different from the slow sand filter by which of the following features?
options: Sand particles are of smaller size
questions.explanation:
Skilled labor is required for rapid sand filters. Unskilled labor is enough for slow sand filters. Comparison of rapid and slow sand filters:
 | Rapid sand filter | Slow sand filter
Space | Occupies very little space | Occupies large area
Rate of filtration (million gall ons per acre per day) | 200 m.g.a.d | 2-3 m.g.a.d.
Effective size of sand | 0.4-0.7 mm | 0.2-0.3 mm
Preliminary treatment | Chemical coagulation and se dimentation | Plain sedimentation
Washing | By back-washing | By scraping the sand be d
Operation | Highly skilled | Less skilled
Loss of head allowed | 6-8 feet (2- 2.5 m) | 4 feet (1.5 m)
Removal of bacteria | 98-99% | 99.9- 99.99%

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a ceramic filter that can be used for small scale purification of water?
questions.explanation:
Filtration of water on a small scale is done by ceramic filters like Pasteur Chamberland, Berkefeld, and Katadyn filters.
Ceramic filters are not widely used in India. The most important parts of these filters are the filter candles. Filter candles of the fine type help in removing bacteria but not viruses. These filter candles need to be cleaned periodically as they get clogged with impurities and bacteria.
Types of ceramic filters include:
Pasteur Chamberland filter – It has a candle made of porcelain. Image of a Pasteur Chamberland filter is shown below:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
Berkefeld filter - it has a candle made of infusorial earth or kieselguhr. Image of a Berkefeld filter is shown below:
Katadyn filter - the surface of this filter is coated with a silver catalyst. The incoming bacteria are killed on contact with the surface by the oligodynamic action of silver ions which are liberated into the water.
Image of a Katadyn filter is shown below:
[[IMG:3]]

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about ceramic filters?
options: Surface of Berkefeld filter is lined with a silver catalyst
Chamberland filter has a porcelain filter candle
Oligodynamic action is seen with Katadyn filter
They are not widely used in India
questions.explanation:
Berkefeld filter has a candle made of infusorial earth or kieselguhr.
Ceramic filters are used for small scale purification of water. They are not widely used in India. The most important parts of these filters are the filter candles.
Types of ceramic filters include:
Pasteur Chamberland filter – It has a candle made of porcelain.
Berkefeld filter - it has a candle made of infusorial earth or kieselguhr.
Katadyn filter - the surface of this filter is coated with a silver catalyst. The incoming bacteria are killed on contact with the surface by the oligodynamic action of silver ions which are liberated into the water.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the method of choice for the purification of highly polluted water on a large scale?
questions.explanation: Superchlorination followed by dechlorination is done for purification of highly polluted water on a large scale.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding chlorination of water?
options: Orthotolidine test measures only combined chlorine
Chlorine acts best when the pH of water is around seven
It kills bacteria, viruses, spores and slime organisms
Hypochlorite ions are mainly responsible for its disinfectant activity
questions.explanation:
Chlorine acts best when the pH of water is around seven because of the predominance of the hypochlorous acid. Most water sources have a pH around 6.5–7, making chlorination an effective form of disinfection.
Option A: Orthotolidine test measures both free and combined chlorine in water.
Option C: Chlorination kills pathogenic bacteria, but has no effect on spores and certain viruses. Option D: The disinfecting action of chlorine is mainly due to hypochlorous acid.

questions.stem: You assign a male health worker at a sub-centre with the task of chlorinating public water resources. What is the minimum concentration of free residual chlorine that should be maintained for effective chlorination?
options: 0.5 mg/litre for a contact period of 1 hour
0.5 mg/litre for a contact period of ½ hour
0.8 mg/litre for a contact period of 1 hour
0.8 mg/litre for a contact period of ½ hour
questions.explanation: The minimum recommended concentration of free residual chlorine for routine chlorination is 0.5 mg/litre for a contact period of 1 hour.

questions.stem: As an epidemiologist, you are investigating an outbreak of cholera. What is the minimum free residual chlorine level that should be maintained in pipelines to prevent further spread of the outbreak?
questions.explanation:
The minimum level of free residual chlorine to be maintained in pipelines following an outbreak of cholera is 0.5 mg/litre.
After a disaster (such as a flood), the water bodies are contaminated with sewage and drainage. The mixing of faeces in drinking bodies increases the risk of numerous microbial infections. The advisable level of free residual chlorine in water bodies after a disaster is, therefore, higher
i.e. 0.7-0.9 mg/litre.

questions.stem: The municipal corporation in your area is performing routine chlorination of drinking water supplies. Which of the following statements about chlorination is incorrect?
options: Free chlorine is released in water after breakpoint chlorination
Chlorine demand is the amount needed to kill spores, protozoal cysts and helminthic ova
0.5 ppm of free chlorine must be present in water after the breakpoint has been reached
Contact period of 1 hour is necessary
questions.explanation:
Chlorine demand is the amount of chlorine that is needed to kill bacteria, and to oxidize all the organic matter and ammoniacal substances in the water. It is the difference between the amount of chlorine added to the water and the amount of residual chlorine remaining at the end of a specific period of contact (usually 1 hour) at a given temperature and pH of the water.
0.5 ppm (0.5 mg) of free chlorine must be present in water after the breakpoint has been reached.

questions.stem: Which of the following tests identifies free and combined chlorine in water separately?
questions.explanation:
Orthotolidine-arsenite test determines both free and combined chlorine in water separately. Orthotolidine test determines free and combined chlorine together.
Chick Martin test and Garrod's test are used to test the efficacy of disinfectants.

questions.stem: Which of the following compounds is predominantly responsible for the disinfecting property of bleaching powder?
questions.explanation:
The disinfectant property of bleaching powder is predominantly due to the action of hypochlorous acid. It is 70-80 times more effective than hypochlorite ions.
Bleaching powder, also known as chlorinated lime (CaOCl2), has 33 per cent of chlorine in it. When chlorine is added to water, there is the formation of hydrochloric and hypochlorous acids. The hydrochloric acid is neutralized by the alkalinity of the water. The hypochlorous acid ionizes to form hydrogen ions and hypochlorite ions, as follows:
H2O + Cl2  HCl + HOCl HOCl  H + OCl

questions.stem: A village health and sanitation team is planning to disinfect 100 wells. Which of the following is the most cost-effective method in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Disinfection of wells using bleaching powder is the most widely used and cheapest method.

questions.stem: An outbreak of viral hepatitis A has been reported in a village. On investigating, you find a contaminated well in the locality to be the source of the outbreak. Which of the following methods would you advise for chlorinating the well in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
The double pot method is used for disinfecting wells by chlorination in emergencies like hepatitis A outbreak in a village.
Double pot method has an inner and outer pot, each with a hole in it and covered with a polyethylene foil. The inner pot is filled with bleaching powder and coarse sand. The double pot system is then lowered into a well. This device can work satisfactorily for 2 – 3 weeks in small wells containing about 4500 litres of water.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: In your community medicine practicals, you are given an apparatus as shown in the image given below. Which of the following statements regarding the apparatus is true? [[IMG:1]]
options: The indicator used is bromocresol purple
It is used to estimate free chlorine levels
It is used to estimate combined chlorine levels
questions.explanation:
The image given is that of a Horrock's apparatus. The indicator used in Horrock's apparatus is starch iodide.
Horrock's apparatus contains 6 white cups (200 ml each), 1 black cup with a circular mark, 2 metal spoons with 2 grams of bleaching powder in each, 7 glass stirring rods, 1 special pipette and 2 droppers. It is not usful in measuring free and combined chlorine. It estimates the chlorine demand of water and is used to calculate the amount of bleaching powder used to disinfect the well.

questions.stem: What is the amount of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 litres of water if the 4th, 5th, and 6th cups of a Horrock’s apparatus show distinct blue color?
questions.explanation:
The dose of bleaching powder required is 8 grams.
It is given by (n x 2) gms for 455 litres of water, where n is the number of the first cup that shows distinct blue color. In this scenario, the dose of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 litres of water is (4 x 2) = 8grams.

questions.stem: The water sample from a well is tested using Horrock’s apparatus. It is observed that the 3rd cup shows a blue color after the addition of the starch-iodine indicator. How much bleaching powder will be required to disinfect 2275 litres of the well water?
questions.explanation:
The dose of bleaching powder required is 30 grams.
It is given by (n x 2) gms for 455 liters of water, where n is the number of the first cup that shows a distinct blue color.
In this scenario, the dose of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 liters of water is (3 x 2) = 6 grams.
Since 2275/455 = 5. The amount of bleaching powder required to disinfect 2275 litres of water = 6 x 5 = 30 grams.

questions.stem: Which of the following agents have residual germicidal effect when used for treatment of water?
questions.explanation:
Chlorine has residual germicidal effect when used for treatment of water.
UV radiation, ozone gas, iodine and potassium permanganate have good germicidal action but do not have residual germicidal effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties of ozone makes it less suitable for the disinfection of water on a large scale?
options: Ozone requires a long time period for action
It has no residual disinfectant action
questions.explanation:
Ozone has no residual disinfectant action.
Ozone gas can be used as a primary disinfectant of water in a large scale. Ozone disinfection is usually followed by biological filtration or granular activated carbon to prevent further contamination during distribution. Chlorine residual treatment is also done as ozone does not provide for a residual disinfectant action.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a lower-pressure membrane process for treatment of water?
questions.explanation:
Microfiltration is a lower-pressure membrane process used for the treatment of water.
Membrane processes are employed in the large scale treatment of water. They are classified as high-pressure processes and lower-pressure processes.
High-pressure processes:
Reverse osmosis - Rejects monovalent ions and organic molecules of molecular weight > 50 daltons. It is most commonly used for desalination of brackish water and sea water. The membrane pore size is < 0.002 µm.
Nanofiltration - Allows monovalent ions such as sodium or potassium to pass but rejects a high proportion of divalent ions like calcium and magnesium and some higher molecular weight organics. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.001 – 0.01 µm.
Lower-pressure processes:
Ultrafiltration - Rejects organic molecules of molecular weight > 800 daltons. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.002 - 0.003 µm.
Microfiltration - Rejects colloidal and suspended material. It does not separate molecules and is usually used before reverse osmosis. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.01 – 12 µm.

chapters.title: Water - III: Water Quality and Standards

questions.stem: Above what level does the turbidity of water become visible to the naked eye?
questions.explanation:
Turbidity of water becomes visible to the naked eye above 4 nephelometric turbidity units (NTU).
The ideal level of turbidity is <1.0 NTU for household drinking purposes. However, in situations where this is not achievable, the maximum permissible limit is <5 NTU.

questions.stem: What is the maximum permissible level of chloride in drinking water?
questions.explanation: The maximum permissible level of chloride in drinking water is 600 mg/litre.

questions.stem: A detectable taste begins to appear in drinking water if chloride levels in it exceed:
questions.explanation: A detectable taste begins to appear in drinking water if chloride levels in it exceed 250 mg/litre.

questions.stem: A large number of cases of methemoglobinemia were reported among infants from a municipal area. On detailed investigation, the nitrate levels in drinking water were found to be elevated in that area. This complication can occur when nitrate level in drinking water exceeds:
questions.explanation: Nitrates in the excess of 45 mg/L may cause methaemoglobinemia in infants.

questions.stem: Which is the most undesirable metal in drinking water?
questions.explanation: The most undesirable metal in drinking water is lead.

questions.stem: What is the acceptable level of total dissolved solids in drinking water in India?
questions.explanation:
According to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the acceptable level of total dissolved solids
(TDS) in drinking water in India is 500 mg/L.
Note: There is a variation in the value of the acceptable level of total dissolved solids in drinking water provided by WHO and the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). While the WHO sets the value at 600 mg/L, the BIS has set it at 500 mg/L for India.

questions.stem: Multiple tube method is done for which of the following?

questions.explanation:
The multiple tube method is done to detect the presence of coliform organisms in a sample of water.
In order to estimate the presumptive coliform count, water to be tested is inoculated into tubes containing a suitable liquid medium. These tubes are then incubated and examined after an appropriate period of time. The test is called presumptive because the reaction observed in the tube may occasionally be due to other organisms.
The proportion of false-positive reactions obtained depends both on the bacterial flora of the water under examination and the medium used. Lactose broth, or MacConkey's broth,
with bromocresol purple as an indicator and a standardized concentration of bile salts incubated between 35°C–37°C for 48 hours, seems to be the most suitable media for presumptive tests.

questions.stem: What is ventilation provided by wind blowing through a space called?
questions.explanation:
Ventilation provided by wind blowing through a space is called perflation. Ventilation can be broadly classified as natural and mechanical:
Natural ventilation includes:
Perflation is the ventilation of a space achieved by allowing wind to blow through it and removing the obstacles for this to happen (e.g., opening windows and doors).
Aspiration occurs when there is an obstruction as wind bypasses it and creates a suction action
Diffusion is the passage of air through small spaces or openings
Cross-ventilation is when air is allowed a natural path through the space by providing openings at appropriate places, opposite each other.
The drawback of natural ventilation is that regulation of air quality is not possible. Mechanical ventilation includes:
Exhaust ventilation utilizes exhaust fans placed high up near the roof on the external walls. A vacuum is created by which fresh air enters the ventilated space.
Plenum ventilation uses centrifugal fans to blow fresh air into the room and create a positive pressure, by which vitiated air is pushed out.
Balanced ventilation is the combination of both exhaust and plenum methods of ventilation.
Air conditioning can be done through mechanical ventilation. It is the simultaneous control of all or at least three factors that influence air quality in a confined room or space. These factors include temperature, humidity, air movement, distribution, dust, bacteria, odours and toxic gases.

In living rooms, the daylight factor should be at least 8% and in kitchens, it should be 10%.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a unit of absorbed dose of radiation?
questions.explanation: Rad is a unit of absorbed dose of radiation by tissue or material. It has been replaced by the SI unit which is gray (Gy).

questions.stem: What is the SI unit of radiation dose equivalent?
questions.explanation:
The SI unit of radiation dose equivalent is sievert (Sv).
Dose equivalent (‘) = Absorbed dose (D) x Quality factor (Q)
The quality factor depends upon the density of ionization produced in the tissue by radiation. The factor Q for X-rays, -rays and electrons is 1 and that for an alpha particle is 20.

questions.stem: What is the permissible dose of manmade radiation per year?
questions.explanation: The permissible dose of manmade radiation is 5 rads per year.

questions.stem: A young girl who is 1 month pregnant is concerned about a chest X-ray that she had taken 3 weeks back. What is the dose of radiation below which deterministic effects on the fetus are not seen?
questions.explanation:
Deterministic effects on the fetus are not seen below 5 rads or 50 mSv of radiation. Dose limits of radiation exposure are:
Occupational exposure - Effective dose should not exceed 20 mSv/year averaged over 5 consecutive years / 30 mSv in a year.
General public exposure - Effective dose should not exceed 1 mSv/year
Occupational exposure for pregnant staff - Effective dose to the fetus should not exceed 1mSv/year (same as the general public).
For pregnant patients who require diagnostics with exposure to ionising radiation, the radiation protection principles are followed:
The exposure should be justified
The dose should be as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA principle)
The dose limit is not particularly specified as it involves a single time exposure to diagnostic radiation. Usually, the effective dose to the fetus is <1msv and deterministic effects to the fetus are not seen below 50 mSv (5 Rad).

questions.stem: What was the 10 days rule in radiation related to?
questions.explanation:
The 10 days rule in radiation was related to pregnancy. It is aimed at preventing unintentional exposure of the embryo or fetus to radiation.
This rule states that if a radiograph is being done on the abdomen or pelvis of a woman in her childbearing age, then it should be done during the 10 days following the onset of menstruation.
In most situations, there is growing evidence that strict adherence to the "ten-day rule" may be unnecessarily restrictive. Since organogenesis starts 3 to 5 weeks post-conception, it was felt that radiation exposure in early pregnancy couldn't result in malformation. Based on this, it was suggested to do away with the 10-day rule and replace it with a 28-day rule. This means that radiological examination if justified, can be carried throughout the cycle until a period is missed.

questions.stem: Solid wastes generally should not contain:
questions.explanation:

Solid wastes generally contain:

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a method of solid waste or refuse disposal?
questions.explanation:

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most insanitary method of waste disposal?
questions.explanation:

questions.stem: Which method is most appropriate when suitable land for waste disposal is available?
questions.explanation:
Controlled tipping is the most satisfactory method of refuse disposal when suitable land is available.
In this method, waste materials are placed in a trench, compacted, and covered with earth at the end of the day. This method is also called a sanitary landfill. Chemical, bacteriological and physical changes occur in the buried refuse with temperatures rising to over 60 degrees Celsius within 7 days.
Methods used for controlled tipping are:
Trench method
Ramp method
Area method
Sewage farming is also a method of sewage disposal in places where sufficient and suitable land is available. It is also called land treatment or broad irrigation.

questions.stem: In controlled tipping, the amount of land required for the trench method to be practiced for a population of 10,000 is:
questions.explanation:
In controlled tipping, one acre of land is required by the trench method to be practiced for a population of 10,000.
It is also known as a sanitary landfill. It is the most satisfactory method of refuse disposal where suitable land is available. In this method, waste material is placed in a trench or other prepared area. Then, it is adequately compacted and covered with earth at the end of the day.
Methods used in controlled tipping are:
Trench method: Done in places where level ground is available
Ramp method: Well suited where the terrain is moderately sloping
Area method: Used for filling land depressions, disused quarries, and clay pits

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about composting?
options: Bangalore method is an aerobic process
Mechanical composting uses a controlled environment
Nightsoil can also be disposed with composting
Compost has few or no disease-causing pathogens
questions.explanation:
The Bangalore method of composting is an anaerobic process.
Composting is a method of combined disposal of refuse and nightsoil. In this process, organic matter is broken down into compost. It has manure value and few or no disease-causing pathogens.
Bangalore method is an anaerobic method and is also called hot fermentation
process. Trenches with a depth of not more than 90cm are used for this. This is done by spreading a layer of refuse (15 cm thick) at the bottom of the trench and nightsoil (5cm thick) is added next. Layers of refuse and nightsoil are added alternatively till the heap rises to 30cm above ground level. The heap is then covered with excavated earth. At the end of 4 – 6 months, decomposition will be completed.
Mechanical composting is an aerobic process. In this method, compost is manufactured on a large scale by processing raw materials and turning out a finished product. The refuse is first cleared of salvageable materials. It is then pulverised to reduce the size of particles to less than 2 inches. The pulverised refuse is then mixed with sewage, sludge or nightsoil in a rotating machine and incubated.

questions.explanation:
The recommended retention period for a septic tank is 24 hours.
If the retention period is too short, there is insufficient treatment of sewage and if it is too long, then undue septicity results.

questions.stem: What is wastewater without human excreta called?
questions.explanation:
Wastewater that doesn’t contain human excreta is called sullage. It is also called greywater. E.g., waste water from the kitchen.
Sewage is wastewater from a community that contains solid and liquid excreta along with street and yard washings. It is also called blackwater.

questions.stem: What is the average amount of sewage which flows though the sewerage system in 24 hours known as?
questions.explanation: The average amount of sewage which flows though the sewerage system in 24 hours is known as dry weather flow.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not used to express the strength of sewage?
questions.explanation:
E. coli count is not used to express the strength of sewage. The strength of sewage is expressed only in terms of:
Biochemical oxygen demand
Chemical oxygen demand
Suspended solids

questions.stem: What does the biochemical oxygen demand of sewage indicate?
questions.explanation:
Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) indicates the organic content of sewage.
It is defined as the amount of oxygen absorbed by a sample of sewage for aerobic destruction by living microorganisms.
If wastewater contains toxic substances, the organic load is measured by the chemical oxygen demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following values of biochemical oxygen demand would indicate that the sewage is weak?
questions.explanation: Sewage with biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) of 100mg/L would indicate that it is weak. If the BOD is  300 mg/L, sewage is said to be strong.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a part of the primary treatment of sewage?
questions.explanation: Aeration tank is not a part of primary treatment of sewage. It is a part of secondary treatment of sewage.

questions.stem: What is the function of the grit chamber in modern sewage treatment plants?
options: Allow anaerobic auto-digestion of organic matter
questions.explanation: The function of the grit chamber in modern sewage treatment plants is to allow heavier particles in the sewage to settle.

questions.stem: Trickling filter method is used in which of the following?
questions.explanation: The trickling filter method is used in secondary sewage treatment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the heart of the activated sludge process?
questions.explanation: The heart of the activated sludge process is the aeration tanks.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a requirement for an oxidation pond?
questions.explanation:
Aeration is not a requirement for an oxidation pond.
Oxidation ponds are also called waste stabilization ponds or redox ponds or sewage lagoons. They have become a popular method of purifying sewage for small communities. It is usually an open, shallow pool of around 1 – 1.5m depth with an inlet and outlet.
Requisites for an oxidation pond include:
Algae
Saprophytic bacteria
Sunlight
All of the above factors help in the treatment of sewage waste through aerobic and anaerobic processes. The effluent formed can be used for land irrigation or can be forwarded for further treatment.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old lady from a tribal area presented with fever, chills, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 4 days. The peripheral smear of the patient is given below. Which of the following is true about the mosquito which transmits this disease?

questions.explanation: Japanese encephalitis and West Nile fever are transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Chikungunya, yellow fever, and rift valley fever are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.

questions.stem: A banker who is scheduled to travel to Congo is advised to take the yellow fever vaccine. What is the flight range of the mosquito which transmits this disease?
questions.explanation: Yellow fever is transmitted by the Aedes mosquito. Its flight range is 100 metres.

questions.stem: A patient with fever and mucosal bleeding is diagnosed with dengue fever. Which of the following is false about the mosquito which transmits this disease?
options: Development of larva from egg does not require water

questions.stem: A patient presents with blurring of vision and a painless swelling over his left elbow which has gradually been increasing in size over the past 1 year. On examination, he is noted to have patchy depigmentation on his legs. Which of the following vectors transmits the disease he's suffering from?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness. It is transmitted by blackfly.
The usual presentation of onchocerciasis is the formation of a subcutaneous nodule or onchocercoma. It is a firm non-tender nodule arising from bony sites like the scalp, elbow, ribs, and iliac crest. It is associated with pruritus and rashes. Patients also present with patchy depigmentation on the legs called leopard skin.
The presence of microfilaria in the eye causes photophobia and gradual loss of vision. The most severe manifestations are sclerosing keratitis and chorioretinitis which can lead to blindness.
Blackfly is also called Simulium. It has a flight range of almost 100 miles, making control of adult flies difficult. Abate is widely used as a larvicidal insecticide. The image given below shows a blackfly.

questions.stem: Spot the wrongly matched arthropod and disease.

Biting
Deposit of infective materials on skin or food or other objects

questions.stem: A veterinarian with fever, chills, and myalgia is diagnosed with Q fever. Which of the following is the most common reservoir of this disease?
questions.explanation:
Ticks are the most common reservoir of Q fever.
Coxiella burnetii is the causative pathogen. The most commonly identified sources of human infection are farm animals, such as cattle, goats, and sheep.
Infected mammals shed C. burnetii in their urine, feces, milk, and placenta. Human exposure to C. burnetii may occur as a result of inhalation of contaminated aerosols arising from the
placenta or parturient fluids of infected livestock or from contaminated secretions on the surface of newborn animals.
People working with farm animals and veterinarians are at a higher risk of infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not transmitted by hard ticks?

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about the vector in the given image? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given image is of a soft tick. It can withstand starvation for over a year.
The head of the soft tick lies ventrally and it does not have a scutum. It serves as a reservoir for Q fever and transmits relapsing fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about the vector in the given image? [[IMG:1]]
options: Its nymphal stage has seven stages
It lays hundreds of eggs at once
questions.explanation:
The given image is of a hard tick. The hard tick has only one nymphal stage.
It has a hard chitinous shield called the scutum which covers the entire back in males a small portion in the front in females. It feeds night and day and cannot withstand starvation. It lays several hundreds or thousands of eggs in one sitting.

questions.stem: Which of the following are also known as chiggers?
questions.explanation:
Larval forms of trombiculid mites are also known as chiggers.
They are spider-like arthropods which are vectors for scrub typhus. The image given below shows trombiculid mite.
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
648

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is transmitted by the vector shown in the image given below? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]] [[IMG:4]]
questions.explanation:
The given image is of a reduviid bug. It transmits American trypanosomiasis, also known as Chagas disease.
Reduviid bug is also known as the kissing bug or triatomine bug. It lives in cracks, fissures and other spaces in the walls and ceilings of human dwellings. Residual spraying with HCH or dieldrin is used for the control of these bugs.
Option B: African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) is transmitted by the tsetse fly. Option C: Onchocerciasis is transmitted by the blackfly (Simulium).
Option D: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is transmitted by the sandfly.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with complaints of nocturnal pruritus. Examination shows burrows over the skin of his hands. KOH mount prepared from these lesions is given below. Which of the following vectors transmits this disease? 642
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and KOH mount showing the itch mite are suggestive of scabies. It is transmitted by itch mite or Sarcoptes scabiei.
The female parasite burrows into the epidermis where it breeds. It is a small parasite, barely visible to the naked eye, with 4 pairs of legs.
Its life cycle consists of four stages—egg, larva, nymph, and adult stages. Its spread can be through close contact or contaminated clothes.
Benzyl benzoate is very effective as a sarcopticide. HCH, tetmosol, and sulphur ointments are also used.
The image given below shows itch mite.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is not transmitted by mites?
questions.explanation:
Kyasanur forest disease is not transmitted by mites. It is a viral hemorrhagic fever transmitted by hard ticks.
Scabies, scrub typhus, and rickettsial pox are transmitted by mites.

questions.stem: You are given the following slide during your community medicine practicals. Which of the following diseases is not transmitted by this vector? [[IMG:1]] 643
questions.explanation:
The above image is of a head louse. It does not transmit endemic typhus which is transmitted by fleas.
Lice transmit epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, and trench fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is transmitted by lice?
questions.explanation:
Epidemic typhus is transmitted by lice and caused by Rickettsia prowazekii.
Murine typhus is transmitted by the rat flea. Tick typhus is transmitted by a hard tick. Scrub typhus is transmitted by trombiculid mite.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not transmitted by lice?
questions.explanation:
Q fever is not transmitted by lice. It is spread by the inhalation of contaminated aerosols containing Coxiella burnetti.
Soft ticks are the most common reservoirs of Q fever. The aerosols arise from the placenta or parturient fluids of infected livestock or from contaminated secretions on the surface of newborn animals.

questions.stem: Identify the following vector which transmits murine typhus. [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]] 644
questions.explanation: The given image is of a rat flea-Xenopsylla cheopis. It transmits murine typhus.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is not transmitted by rat fleas?
questions.explanation:
Pneumonic plague is not transmitted by rat fleas. It is transmitted by inhalation of aerosolized droplets.
Rat fleas are vectors for murine or endemic typhus, bubonic plague, and hymenolepiasis caused by Hymenolepis nana and Hymenolepis diminuta.

questions.stem: A flea survey is being conducted in an area prone to outbreaks of plague. Which of the following indices is not used for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Incidence of plague is not an index used in flea surveys. Flea indices that are used in flea surveys are:
General flea index
Specific flea index
Percentage incidence of flea species
Rodent infestation rate

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about sand fleas?
questions.explanation:
Sand fleas cause ulcers in the feet.
They are also called jigger or chigoe fleas. The species called Tunga penetrans is of particular importance as it causes tungiasis.
The fertilized female burrows into the skin of the feet, often beneath the nail and causes ulcers. Tetanus and gas gangrene frequently occur because of secondary infection.
They flourish best in sandy soil and are found in the western parts of India. The below image shows a sand flea.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following is transmitted by the vector shown in the image given below? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given image is of a cyclops or water flea. It is the vector for guinea worm disease or dracunculiasis and fish tapeworm infection.
Humans are infected with these diseases by drinking water that contains cyclops. Its average life span is 3 months.
Physical methods like straining and boiling of water can ensure the killing of this
organism. Chemicals that can be used to control cyclops are chlorine, lime, and abate. Biological methods include Gambusia fish and barbel fish.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is not associated with rodents?
questions.explanation:
Ascariasis is not associated with rodents. Diseases related to rodents are:
Bacterial -
Plague
Tularemia
Salmonellosis
Leptospirosis
Rat-bite fever
Viral -
Lassa fever
Encephalitis
Hemorrhagic fever
Rickettsial -
Scrub typhus
Endemic typhus
Rickettsial pox
Parasitic -
Hymenolepis diminuta
Leishmaniasis
Amoebiasis
Trichinosis
Chagas disease
Fungal -
Histoplasmosis
Ringworm

questions.stem: Which of the following would you advise as the best approach to control arthropods?
questions.explanation:
Environmental control is the best approach to control arthropods. The principles of arthropod control include:
Environmental control - Best approach
Chemical control - Use of insecticides, pesticides, etc.
Biological control - Use of larvivorous fish like Gambusia
Genetic control
Newer methods -
Chemosterilants
Insect growth regulators
Sex attractants
Integrated approach involves usage of more than one modality of arthropod control

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best method to control houseflies?
questions.explanation:
The best method to control houseflies is environmental control by the elimination of breeding places.
They have shown resistance to a number of insecticides, including DDT.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an organo-phosphate insecticide?
questions.explanation: Dieldrin is an organo-chlorine insecticide. It is a broad-spectrum insecticide that acts as a contact, stomach, and inhalation poison.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an aryl organo-phosphate insecticide?
questions.explanation: Malathion is an alkyl organophosphate insecticide. It is used as an ultra-low volume spray in mosquito control.

questions.stem: Which of the following insecticides is least toxic to man?
questions.explanation: Among the given options, malathion is the least toxic to man. It is the least toxic organo-phosphate insecticide.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about fenthion?
options: It is used as a residual spray
It is used as a repellent
questions.explanation:
Fenthion is not used as a repellant. A commonly used repellant is N,N-diethyl-m-toluamide
(DEET) that is used for protection from mosquitoes and ticks.
Fenthion is a broad-spectrum insecticide that acts as both contact and stomach poison. It is used as a larvicide in mosquito control and also as a residual spray.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about pyrethrum?
options: Residual action as good as DDT
Can be used synergistically with DDT
questions.explanation:
Pyrethrum does not have a residual action like DDT or other synthetic insecticides. So, most space sprays contain pyrethrum and DDT for synergistic action.
Pyrethrum is a natural insecticide of vegetable origin. It is extracted from the flowers of Chrysanthemum cinerariafolium. It kills adult mosquitoes and other insects instantly on mere contact.

questions.stem: Which of the following cannot be used to describe pyrethrum?
questions.explanation: Pyrethrum is not used as a residual spray. It is a contact and nerve poison that is also used as a space spray.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a synthetic pyrethroid insecticide?
questions.explanation: Permethrin is a synthetic pyrethroid. Pyrethroids are synthetic insecticides, which are derived from naturally occurring pyrethrins. Pyrethroids modify the sodium channels in neuronal membranes and thereby disrupt the electrical signalling in the nervous system.

questions.stem: Which of the following vectors has not shown resistance to synthetic pyrethroids, in a widespread manner in India yet?
questions.explanation: Sandflies (Phlebotomus) have not shown resistance to synthetic pyrethroids, in a widespread manner in India yet.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes DDT?
questions.explanation: DDT is a contact poison that belongs to the organochlorine family. It has been widely used but a number of organisms have become resistant to its effects now.

questions.stem: During a dengue outbreak, the municipal corporation plans a DDT spraying initiative. Which of the following is false about this insecticide?
options: Para-para isomer is the most active fraction
It has residual action up to 18 months
It causes immediate death of insects
questions.explanation:
DDT does not cause the immediate death of insects. It takes several hours for its action to be complete.
It contains 70 – 80% of para-para isomer that is the most active fraction of DDT. It acts on the nervous system of insects. The residual action of DDT may last as long as 18 months depending upon the treated surface.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the usage of Paris green for mosquito control?
options: Harmful in normal doses to man and animals
questions.explanation:
Paris green is very effective against surface-feeding Anopheles.
It is an anti-larval measure and is a stomach poison. It is not harmful in normal doses to man and animals.

questions.stem: Which of the following mosquitoes can be controlled by destroying aquatic plants with herbicides?
questions.explanation: Mansonia mosquitoes breed in water with aquatic vegetation, and destroying this vegetation with herbicides would control this mosquito.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a mosquito anti-larval measure?
questions.explanation:
Pyrethrum is an anti-adult measure and not an anti-larval measure.
Mineral oils, Gambusia, and Paris green are anti-larval measures used in mosquito control.

questions.stem: Which among the following insecticides is most widely used as a space spray?
questions.explanation: The insecticide most widely used as a space spray is pyrethrum.

questions.stem: Match the following methods of mosquito control to the appropriate examples.
options: I – a, II – b, III – c, IV – d
I – b, II – d, III – c, IV – a
I – c, II – a, III – b, IV – d
I – d, II – b, III – a, IV – c
questions.explanation:
The correctly matched methods of mosquito control are:
Method of control | Example
Biological control | Barbados millio ns
Genetic control | Sex distortion
Chemical control | Larvicidal oil
Environmental contr ol | Source reductio n

questions.stem: To curb an outbreak of plague in your locality, the municipal corporation decides to use rodenticides. Which of the following can be given as a single dose for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Zinc phosphide is a single-dose rodenticide that causes death in a one-time exposure.
Acute or single-dose rodenticides are classified according to the precautions that need to be taken before their use:
Those requiring ordinary care - Red squill, norbormide, zinc phosphide
Those requiring maximal precaution - Sodium fluoroacetate, fluoroacetamide and strychnine
Too dangerous for use - Arsenic trioxide, phosphorus, thallium sulphate
Multiple-dose or cumulative rodenticides cause death after multiple times of exposure. Examples include:
Warfarin
Coumafuryl
Diphacinone
Pindone

questions.stem: Which of the following color labels is used to indicate the most hazardous pesticides?
questions.explanation:
The most hazardous pesticides must have labels in red color. Pesticide toxicity labels:
These labels are depicted in the image below.
[[IMG:1]]
Category of Pesticid e | Color of Lab el
Extremely toxic | Bright red
Highly toxic | Bright yello w
Moderately toxic | Bright blue
Slightly toxic | Bright green

questions.stem: What proportion of healthcare waste is hazardous waste?
questions.explanation:
15% of health care waste is hazardous waste. It may be infectious, toxic, or radioactive in nature. The remaining 85% is general, non-hazardous waste.
Bio-medical waste means any waste that is generated during:
Diagnosis, treatment, or immunization of human beings or animals
Research activities pertaining thereto
Production or testing of biologicals
Bio-medical waste is handled as per the Bio-medical Waste Management Rules, 2016. However, these rules do not apply to the following:
Radioactive wastes
Hazardous chemicals
Solid wastes
Lead-acid batteries
Hazardous wastes
e-Waste
Hazardous microorganisms

questions.stem: Cytotoxic and expired drugs are disposed by:
questions.explanation:
Cytotoxic and expired drugs are collected in a yellow bag and then disposed of by incineration.
Expired cytotoxic drugs are to be returned to the manufacturer and subjected to incineration, encapsulation, or plasma pyrolysis. Other discarded medicines can be disposed by incineration.

questions.stem: Which of the following category of wastes are treated by autoclaving and microwaving?
questions.explanation:
The final treatment of catheters, urine bags, and gloves is done by autoclaving and microwaving. They belong to recyclable contaminated waste and are disposed of in a red bag.
Option A: Human anatomical waste is disposed of by incineration.
Option C: Cytotoxic and expired/discarded medicine is disposed of by incineration/plasma pyrolysis/disposal in a secured landfill.
Option D: Microbiological waste such as culture plates and slides are pre-treated with nonchlorinated chemicals and later disposed of by incineration.

questions.stem: While working as a 1st-year resident in the labor ward, where would you dispose of the placenta following a delivery?
questions.explanation: Human anatomical wastes, like the placenta, are discarded in a yellow bag and disposed of by incineration/ plasma pyrolysis/ deep burial.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are true about yellow waste disposal bags?
questions.explanation:
Yellow waste disposal bags are made from non-chlorinated plastic material and chemical liquid wastes are collected in them.
Chlorinated items, glass, metal, and rubber are not sent for incineration as incinerating them would produce carcinogenic gases.
The right disposal methods of the other options are:
Animal anatomical waste - Collected in yellow bags and later sent for incineration.
Metallic body implants - Collected in cardboard boxes with blue coloured marking and sent for recycling following autoclaving.
PVC gloves - Collected in red bags and sent for autoclaving followed by shredding.

questions.stem: Which of the following should not be incinerated?
questions.explanation:
Specimens of microorganisms and live or attenuated vaccines can be incinerated. Wastes that should not be incinerated are:
Sharps
Pressurized gas containers
Reactive chemical waste
Waste with heavy metals like mercury and cadmium
PVC
Photographic or radiographic waste

questions.stem: An orthopedic resident has removed a ‰-wire from the fractured olecranon of a 13-year-old boy. Where should he discard this?
questions.explanation:
Metallic body implants are disposed of in cardboard boxes with blue-colored markings.
The contents of the blue box are sent to Common Biomedical Waste Treatment and Disposal Facility (CBWTF). In the facility, these items are sterilized by autoclaving or microwaving and then sent for recycling.

questions.stem: Blood bag is to be disposed in:
questions.explanation: Blood bag should be disposed off in the yellow bin.

questions.stem: An HIV-positive man is brought to you following an accident. How would you discard his blood-soaked dressing material?
options: Pour 1% hypochlorite on the dressing material and send for incineration
Pour 5% hypochlorite on the dressing material and send for incineration
Put the dressing material directly in an appropriate bag and send for incineration
Pour 10% non chlorinated chemicals on the dressing material and send for incineration
questions.explanation:
The blood-soaked dressing material should be disposed of in a non-chlorinated yellow bag and sent for incineration. Pretreatment is not a requisite for incinerating soiled waste.
Items that require pretreatment with non-chlorinated chemicals before incineration:
Used blood bags
Other infectious plastic and liquid wastes
Laboratory cultures, stocks, or specimens of microorganisms
Live or attenuated vaccines
Human and animal cell cultures used in research
Dishes, and devices used for cultures

questions.stem: Which of the following disposal methods is not as per biomedical waste management guidelines?
options: Disposal of a dead fetus of 21 weeks in a yellow bag by deep burial in rural areas
Pre-treatment of laboratory cultures with non-chlorinated disinfectant
Disposal of a glass ampoule with its cytotoxic drug through incineration
Disposal of radiological waste by deep burial
questions.explanation:
Radiological waste is not considered biomedical waste. Hence, deep burial is not done.
Disposal of radiological is covered under the provisions of the Atomic Energy Act. The radiological effluents are incinerated in a dedicated incinerator having off-gas cleaning facility. Another method is to convert the organic base into an aqueous form by treating it with sodium hydroxide.
Option A: Dead fetuses under the age of viability are considered human anatomical waste. Anatomical waste can be disposed of by deep burial in rural areas, where a common biomedical treatment facility and incineration is not available.
Option B: Laboratory cultures are classified under the category of microbiology, biotechnology, and other clinical laboratory waste. They are pretreated with a non-chlorinated disinfectant before they are sent for incineration.
Option C: The cytotoxic drugs are disposed of along with their packaging, through incineration.

questions.stem: You are asked to catheterize an HBsAg-positive man before hernia surgery. According to the BMW management rules, where would you dispose of the plastic cover of the catheter?
questions.explanation:
The outer plastic cover of the Foleys catheter is discarded in a black bag.
Foleys catheters are packaged in plastic covers to keep them sterile. The plastic cover is not biomedical waste but is a part of general (municipal) waste. Hence, it is discarded in the black bag. The foleys catheter is disposed of in a red bag.
As per Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, the general waste must be disposed of in green bins (for recyclable waste) and blue bins (for non-recyclable waste) containing black plastic bags.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases should healthcare workers involved in handling biomedical waste be vaccinated against?
questions.explanation:
Healthcare workers involved in handling biomedical waste should be vaccinated against hepatitis B and tetanus.
These are most likely to be transmitted by the handling of biomedical waste. Yearly health check-ups should be done, and a booster dose should be given if needed.

questions.stem: An on-site waste treatment and disposal facility should be built in a hospital if the nearest common biomedical treatment facility is:
questions.explanation:
According to biomedical waste management rules of 2016, healthcare establishments shall establish an on-site treatment and disposal facility only when a common biomedical treatment facility (CBMWTF) is more than 75 km away.
According to these rules, biomedical waste (BMW) from healthcare facilities is to be transported to a CMBWTF. The establishment of CBMWTF reduces the need for transport and cost of treatment/ kg of BMW.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a high-heat system for the treatment of biomedical waste?
questions.explanation:
Microwaving is a low-heat system for the treatment of biomedical waste.
The heating systems used for the treatment and disposal of biomedical waste are:
Low-heat system | High-heat system
Autoclaving:Uses steam. It is of two types-Gravity flow aut oclaveVacuum autoclaveMicr owaving:Uses moist heat and steam generated by microwa ve energy | Incineration:Waste is destroy ed/denatured under high tem peraturesPlasma pyrolysis:W aste is treated at high temper atures under controlled condi tions to form gases that are s ubjected to combustion in th e secondary chamberHydrocl aving:The waste is subjected to indirect heating by applyin g steam to the outer jacketDr y heat sterilization:Waste sha rps are treated using dry heat at a temperature >185 C for 150 minutes

questions.stem: Which of the following disposal methods uses high temperature and dry oxidation?
questions.explanation:
Incineration is a high-temperature dry oxidation process.
Waste that is incinerated need not undergo any type of pre-treatment. It helps to reduce weight as well as volume. The temperature in the incinerator is 800■C in the primary chamber and 1050■C in the secondary chamber.
Types of incinerators:
Rotary kilns
Single chamber pyrolytic
Double chamber pyrolytic
The heating systems used for the treatment and disposal of biomedical waste are:
Low-heat system | High-heat system
Autoclaving:Uses steam. It is of two types-Gravity flow aut oclaveVacuum autoclaveMicr owaving:Uses moist heat and steam generated by microwa ve energy | Incineration:Waste is destroy ed/denatured under high tem peraturesPlasma pyrolysis:W aste is treated at high temper atures under controlled condi tions to form gases that are s ubjected to combustion in th e secondary chamberHydrocl aving:The waste is subjected to indirect heating by applyin g steam to the outer jacketDr y heat sterilization:Waste sha rps are treated using dry heat at a temperature >185 C for 150 minutes

questions.stem: In a treatment facility, which of the following cannot be used to verify the treatment of biomedical waste done by incineration?
questions.explanation:
Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis is not used to verify thermal methods of biomedical waste disposal. It is a biological larvicide, used in nonpotable water for killing mosquito larvae.
The following can be used to verify the adequacy of thermal methods of biomedical waste disposal:
Bacillus atropheus
Bacillus subtilis
Geobacillus stearothermophilus

questions.stem: At a waste treatment facility, pharmaceutical waste was mixed with cement, lime, and water before disposal. What is this method known as?
questions.explanation:
Inertization is the process of mixing biomedical waste with non-toxic substances to reduce the toxicity of the waste and to reduce the contamination of groundwater. It is most commonly done for incineration ash with high metal content.
The typical composition of the inertization mixture is:
65% pharmaceutical waste
15% cement
15% lime
5% water

questions.stem: What is the correct combination of temperature and duration used in a hot air oven?
questions.explanation:
The correct combinations of temperature and duration of sterilisation in a hot air oven is:
180°C for 30 mins
170°C for 60 mins
160■C for 2 hours
It can be used to sterilize powders, glasswares, and oils.
An autoclave is another apparatus that is used for sterilization. It uses steam at a temperature of 121■C for 30 mins under 15 lbs of pressure.

questions.stem: All the following are the characteristics of waste that can be incinerated except:
questions.explanation:
Only waste material containing <5% of noncombustible solids can be incinerated. Wastes that are incinerated go in the yellow bag.
Waste products with the following characteristics can be incinerated:
Combustible matter >60%
Non-combustible solid <5%
Non-combustible fine <20%
Low heating volume
Moisture content <30%.

questions.explanation:
